## Rick D. Husband

Commander

Rick Husband, 45, a colonel in the U.S. Air Force, was a test pilot and veteran of one spaceflight. He served as commander for STS-107. Husband received a bachelor of science in mechanical engineering from Texas Tech University in 1980 and a master of science in mechanical engineering from California State University-Fresno in 1990. As commander, Husband was responsible for the overall conduct of the mission. During the mission, he maneuvered Columbia as part of several experiments in the shuttle’s payload bay that focused on the Earth and the Sun. He was also the senior member of the Red Team and worked with the following experiments: European Research In Space and Terrestrial Osteoporosis (ERISTO); Mediterranean Israeli Dust Experiment (MEIDEX); Osteoporosis Experiment in Orbit (OSTEO); the Physiology and Biochemistry Team (PhAB4) suite of experiments, which included Calcium Kinetics, Latent Virus Shedding, Protein Turnover and Renal Stone Risk; and Shuttle Ozone Limb Sounding Experiment (SOLSE-2).  
  
Selected by NASA in December 1994, Husband served as the pilot of STS-96 in 1999 – a 10-day mission during which the crew performed the first docking with the International Space Station. Prior to STS-107, Husband logged more than 235 hours in space.

## William C. McCool

Pilot

William C. McCool, 41, a commander in the U.S. Navy, was a former test pilot. He served as pilot for STS-107. He received a bachelor of science in applied science from the U.S. Naval Academy in 1983, a master of science in computer science from the University of Maryland in 1985, and a master of science in aeronautical engineering from the U.S. Naval Postgraduate School in 1992. McCool, as a member of the Blue Team, worked with the following experiments: European Space Agency (ESA) Advanced Respiratory Monitoring System (ARMS); ESA Biopack (eight experiments); Mediterranean Israeli Dust Experiment (MEIDEX); and the Physiology and Biochemistry Team (PhAB4) suite of experiments, which included Calcium Kinetics, Latent Virus Shedding, Protein Turnover and Renal Stone Risk. He was also responsible for maneuvering Columbia as part of several experiments mounted in the shuttle’s payload bay.  
  
Selected by NASA in April 1996, McCool was making his first spaceflight.

## Michael P. Anderson

Payload Commander

Michael P. Anderson, 43, a lieutenant colonel in the U.S. Air Force, was a former instructor pilot and tactical officer, and a veteran of one spaceflight. He served as Payload Commander and Mission Specialist 3 for STS-107. As payload commander he was responsible for the success (management) of the science mission aboard STS-107. Anderson received a bachelor of science in physics/astronomy from University of Washington in 1981 and a master of science in physics from Creighton University in 1990. Anderson, as a member of the Blue Team, worked with the following experiments: European Space Agency Advanced Respiratory Monitoring System (ARMS); Combustion Module (CM-2), which included the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP), Water Mist Fire Suppression (MIST) and Structures of Flame Balls at Low Lewis-number (SOFBALL) experiments; Mediterranean Israeli Dust Experiment (MEIDEX); Mechanics of Granular Materials (MGM); and the Physiology and Biochemistry Team (PhAB4) suite of experiments, which included Calcium Kinetics, Latent Virus Shedding, Protein Turnover and Renal Stone Risk.  
  
Selected by NASA in December 1994, Anderson flew on STS-89 in 1998 – the eighth Shuttle-Mir docking mission. Prior to STS-107, Anderson logged over 211 hours in space.

## David Brown

Mission Specialist 1

David M. Brown, 46, a captain in the U.S. Navy, was a naval aviator and flight surgeon. He served as Mission Specialist 1 for STS-107. Brown received a bachelor of science in biology from the College of William and Mary in 1978 and a doctorate in medicine from Eastern Virginia Medical School in 1982. Brown, as a member of the Blue Team, worked with the following experiments: European Space Agency Advanced Respiratory Monitoring System (ARMS); Combustion Module (CM-2), which included the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP), Water Mist Fire Suppression (MIST) and Structures of Flame Balls at Low Lewis-number (SOFBALL) experiments; Mediterranean Israeli Dust Experiment (MEIDEX); and the Physiology and Biochemistry Team (PhAB4) suite of experiments, which included Calcium Kinetics, Latent Virus Shedding, Protein Turnover and Renal Stone Risk.  
  
Selected by NASA in April 1996, Brown was making his first spaceflight.

## Kalpana Chawla

Mission Specialist 2

Kalpana Chawla, 41, was an aerospace engineer and an FAA Certified Flight Instructor. Chawla served as Flight Engineer and Mission Specialist 2 for STS-107. She received a bachelor of science in aeronautical engineering from Punjab Engineering College, India, in 1982, a master of science in aerospace engineering from the University of Texas-Arlington in 1984, and a doctorate in aerospace engineering from the University of Colorado-Boulder in 1988. As a member of the Red Team, Chawla, with CDR Rick Husband, was responsible for maneuvering Columbia as part of several experiments in the shuttle’s payload bay. Chawla also worked with the following experiments: Astroculture (AST); Advanced Protein Crystal Facility (APCF); Commercial Protein Crystal Growth (CPCG_PCF); Biotechnology Demonstration System (BDS); ESA Biopack (eight experiments); Combustion Module (CM-2), which included the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP), Water Mist Fire Suppression (MIST) and Structures of Flame Balls at Low Lewisnumber (SOFBALL) experiments; Mechanics of Granular Materials (MGM); Vapor Compression Distillation Flight Experiment (VCD FE); and the Zeolite Crystal Growth Furnace (ZCG).  
  
Selected by NASA in December 1994, Chawla was the prime robotic arm operator on STS-87 in 1997, the fourth U.S. Microgravity Payload flight. STS-87 focused on how the weightless environment of space affects various physical processes. Prior to STS-107, Chawla logged more than 376 hours in space.

## Laurel Blair Salton Clark

Mission Specialist

Laurel Clark, 41, a commander (captain-select) in the U.S. Navy and a naval flight surgeon, was Mission Specialist 4 on STS-107. Clark received a bachelor of science in zoology from the University of Wisconsin-Madison in 1983 and a doctorate in medicine from the same school in 1987. Clark, as a member of the Red Team, worked with the following experiments: European Space Agency (ESA) Advanced Respiratory Monitoring System (ARMS); Astroculture (AST-1 and 2); Biotechnology Demonstration System (BDS); ESA Biopack (eight experiments); Application of Physical & Biological Techniques to Study the Gravisensing and Response System of Plants: Magnetic Field Apparatus (Biotube-MFA); Closed Equilibrated Biological Aquatic System (CEBAS); Commercial ITA Biological Experiments (CIBX); the Microbial Physiology Flight Experiments Team (MPFE) experiments, which included the Effects of Microgravity on Microbial Physiology and Spaceflight Effects on Fungal Growth, Metabolism and Sensitivity to Antifungal Drugs; Osteoporosis Experiment in Orbit (OSTEO); the Physiology and Biochemistry Team (PhAB4) suite of experiments, which included Calcium Kinetics, Latent Virus Shedding, Protein Turnover and Renal Stone Risk; Sleep-Wake Actigraphy and Light Exposure During Spaceflight (SLEEP); and the Vapor Compression Distillation Flight Experiment (VCD FE).  
  
Selected by NASA in April 1996, Clark was making her first spaceflight.

## Ilan Ramon

Payload Specialist 1

Ilan Ramon, 48, a colonel in the Israeli Air Force, was a fighter pilot who was the only payload specialist on STS-107. Ramon received a bachelor of science in electronics and computer engineering from the University of Tel Aviv, Israel, in 1987. Ramon, as a member of the Red Team, was the prime crewmember for the Mediterranean Israeli Dust Experiment (MEIDEX), a multispectral camera that measured small dust particles (dust aerosols) in the atmosphere over the Mediterranean and the Saharan coast of the Atlantic. He worked with the following experiments: European Space Agency Advanced Respiratory Monitoring System (ARMS); Astroculture (AST-1 and 2); Biological Research in Canister – Development of Gravity Sensitive Plant Cells in Microgravity (BRIC); Combustion Module (CM-2), which included the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP), Water Mist Fire Suppression (MIST) and Structures of Flame Balls at Low Lewis-number (SOFBALL) experiments; the Microbial Physiology Flight Experiments Team (MPFE) experiments, which included the Effects of Microgravity on Microbial Physiology and Spaceflight Effects on Fungal Growth, Metabolism and Sensitivity to Anti-fungal Drugs; the Physiology and Biochemistry Team (PhAB4) suite of experiments, which included Calcium Kinetics, Latent Virus Shedding, Protein Turnover and Renal Stone Risk; and Space Technology and Research Students Bootes (STARS Bootes).  
  
Ramon was selected as a Payload Specialist by the Israeli Air Force in 1997 and approved by NASA in 1998. He reported for training at the NASA Johnson Space Center in Houston in July 1998 and was making his first spaceflight.

**Preface**

NASA selected the first group of astronauts in 1959. From 500 candidates having the required jet aircraft flight experience and engineering training, as well as height below 5 feet 11 inches, seven military men became the nation’s first astronauts. The second and third groups chosen included civilians with extensive flying experience. By 1964, requirements changed, and emphasis was placed on academic qualifications; in 1965, six scientist astronauts were selected from a group of 400 applicants who had a doctorate or equivalent experience in the natural sciences, medicine, or engineering. The group named in 1978, NASA Class 8, was the first of the space shuttle flight crews and the first class with women and minority astronauts. In 2013, the astronaut class was fifty percent women and fifty percent men.

The most recent astronaut candidate group named in September 2025, NASA Class 24, are currently completing nearly two years of training before becoming eligible for flight assignments supporting future science and exploration missions to low Earth orbit, the Moon, and Mars. The 2025 astronaut candidate class came from more than 8,000 applications. More information about NASA’s astronauts can be found at [www.nasa.gov/astronauts](http://www.nasa.gov/astronauts).

Since inception, NASA has selected 370 astronaut candidates: 303 men, 67 women; 226 military, 144 civilians; 203 pilots, 167 non-pilots.

As of August 2026, there are 35 active astronauts, 9 management astronauts, 10 astronaut candidates, and 344 former astronauts or payload specialists, including those who have left NASA, and those who are deceased.

The spaceflights and statistics listed in this publication resulted from the vertical takeoff of an American space vehicle or Soyuz taxi flight to the International Space Station.

Astronauts listed (unless otherwise noted) are individuals who participated in the United States astronaut program. Additionally, the payload specialist is a professional in the physical or life sciences or a technician skilled in specific equipment or experimentation that will fly. Selection of a payload specialist for a mission is made by the payload sponsor or customer. For NASA-sponsored spacecraft or experiments requiring a payload specialist, the specialist is nominated by an investigator working group and approved by NASA. Payload specialists for major non-NASA payloads or experiments are selected by the sponsoring organization. Payload specialists do not have to be U.S. citizens. However, they must meet strict NASA health and physical fitness standards. These individuals are included in the “Biographical Sketches.”

NASA selects astronauts from a diverse pool of applicants with a wide variety of backgrounds. From the thousands of applications received, only a few are chosen for the intensive astronaut candidate training program. For more information on astronaut selection, please check online at [www.nasa.gov/astronauts](http://www.nasa.gov/astronauts) for the latest information.

Astronaut biographies can be found online at: [https://www.nasa.gov/astronauts](https://www.nasa.gov/astronauts).

**Preface**

NASA selected the first group of astronauts in 1959. From 500 candidates having the required jet aircraft flight experience and engineering training, as well as height below 5 feet 11 inches, seven military men became the nation’s first astronauts. The second and third groups chosen included civilians with extensive flying experience. By 1964, requirements changed, and emphasis was placed on academic qualifications; in 1965, six scientist astronauts were selected from a group of 400 applicants who had a doctorate or equivalent experience in the natural sciences, medicine, or engineering. The group named in 1978, NASA Class 8, was the first of the space shuttle flight crews and the first class with women and minority astronauts. In 2013, the astronaut class was fifty percent women and fifty percent men.

The most recent astronaut candidate group named in September 2025, NASA Class 24, are currently completing nearly two years of training before becoming eligible for flight assignments supporting future science and exploration missions to low Earth orbit, the Moon, and Mars. The 2025 astronaut candidate class came from more than 8,000 applications. More information about NASA’s astronauts can be found at [www.nasa.gov/astronauts](http://www.nasa.gov/astronauts).

Since inception, NASA has selected 370 astronaut candidates: 303 men, 67 women; 226 military, 144 civilians; 203 pilots, 167 non-pilots.

As of August 2026, there are 35 active astronauts, 9 management astronauts, 10 astronaut candidates, and 344 former astronauts or payload specialists, including those who have left NASA, and those who are deceased.

The spaceflights and statistics listed in this publication resulted from the vertical takeoff of an American space vehicle or Soyuz taxi flight to the International Space Station.

Astronauts listed (unless otherwise noted) are individuals who participated in the United States astronaut program. Additionally, the payload specialist is a professional in the physical or life sciences or a technician skilled in specific equipment or experimentation that will fly. Selection of a payload specialist for a mission is made by the payload sponsor or customer. For NASA-sponsored spacecraft or experiments requiring a payload specialist, the specialist is nominated by an investigator working group and approved by NASA. Payload specialists for major non-NASA payloads or experiments are selected by the sponsoring organization. Payload specialists do not have to be U.S. citizens. However, they must meet strict NASA health and physical fitness standards. These individuals are included in the “Biographical Sketches.”

NASA selects astronauts from a diverse pool of applicants with a wide variety of backgrounds. From the thousands of applications received, only a few are chosen for the intensive astronaut candidate training program. For more information on astronaut selection, please check online at [www.nasa.gov/astronauts](http://www.nasa.gov/astronauts) for the latest information.

Astronaut biographies can be found online at: [https://www.nasa.gov/astronauts](https://www.nasa.gov/astronauts).

**Michael Phillip Anderson** (December 25, 1959 – February 1, 2003) was a [United States Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force") officer and [NASA astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_astronaut "NASA astronaut"). He and his six fellow crew members were killed in the [Space Shuttle _Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") when the [craft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")[disintegrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In-flight_breakup "In-flight breakup") during its [re-entry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reentry_(orbital) "Reentry (orbital)") into the [Earth's atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_atmosphere "Earth's atmosphere").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:4-1) Anderson served as the payload commander and lieutenant colonel in charge of science experiments on the _Columbia_. He was posthumously awarded the [Congressional Space Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Space_Medal_of_Honor "Congressional Space Medal of Honor").

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Michael Philip Anderson was born in [Plattsburgh, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plattsburgh,_New_York "Plattsburgh, New York") on December 25, 1959, to Barbara and Bobbie Anderson. He was their third child and only son. Bobbie serviced jets at [Plattsburgh Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plattsburgh_Air_Force_Base "Plattsburgh Air Force Base") in Plattsburgh[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) and was transferred to [Fairchild Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairchild_Air_Force_Base "Fairchild Air Force Base"), about 12 miles (19 km) away from [Spokane, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spokane,_Washington "Spokane, Washington"), which Anderson spoke of as his hometown.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:1-3) Anderson graduated from [Cheney High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheney_School_District "Cheney School District") in [Cheney, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheney,_Washington "Cheney, Washington"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-4) one of four [African Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans") in a class of 200 students.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

In 1981, Anderson graduated with a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physics "Physics") and [astronomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomy "Astronomy") from the [University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington") in [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle"). In 1990, he earned a [Master of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") degree in physics from [Creighton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creighton_University "Creighton University") in [Omaha, Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omaha,_Nebraska "Omaha, Nebraska").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-5)

## Air Force career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Air Force career")]

Upon Anderson's graduation from the University of Washington, he was commissioned a [second lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Lieutenant "Second Lieutenant") in the [U.S. Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Air_Force "U.S. Air Force").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) After completing a year of technical training at [Keesler Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keesler_Air_Force_Base "Keesler Air Force Base") in [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi"), Anderson was assigned to [Randolph Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randolph_Air_Force_Base "Randolph Air Force Base") in [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) At Randolph, he served as chief of communication maintenance for the 2015th Communication Squadron and later as director of information system maintenance for the 1920th Information System Group.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

In 1986, Anderson was selected to attend [Undergraduate Pilot Training](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undergraduate_Pilot_Training "Undergraduate Pilot Training") at [Vance Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vance_Air_Force_Base "Vance Air Force Base"), [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) Upon graduation, he was assigned to the [2d Airborne Command and Control Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2d_Airborne_Command_and_Control_Squadron "2d Airborne Command and Control Squadron"), [Offutt Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offutt_Air_Force_Base "Offutt Air Force Base"), [Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebraska "Nebraska") as an [EC-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_EC-135 "Boeing EC-135") pilot, flying the [Strategic Air Command](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_Air_Command "Strategic Air Command")'s airborne command post code-named "[Looking Glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Looking_Glass "Operation Looking Glass")." Anderson completed his master's degree while stationed at Offutt.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

From January 1991 to September 1992, Anderson served as an aircraft commander and [instructor pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_instructor "Flight instructor") in the [920th Air Refueling Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/920th_Air_Refueling_Squadron "920th Air Refueling Squadron"), [Wurtsmith Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wurtsmith_Air_Force_Base "Wurtsmith Air Force Base"), [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan "Michigan").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

From September 1992 to February 1995, Anderson was assigned as an instructor pilot and tactics officer in the [380th Air Refueling Wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/380th_Air_Refueling_Wing "380th Air Refueling Wing"), [Plattsburgh Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plattsburgh_Air_Force_Base "Plattsburgh Air Force Base"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

Anderson logged more than 3,000 hours of flight time when NASA selected him for astronaut training in December 1994.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) Anderson was one of 19 candidates selected from a pool of 2,962 applicants.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

## NASA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: NASA")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Michael_P._Anderson.jpg/250px-Michael_P._Anderson.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Michael_P._Anderson.jpg)

Anderson in 1995

Anderson reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in March 1995.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) He completed a year of training and evaluation, and was qualified for flight crew assignment as a [mission specialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_Specialist "Mission Specialist").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) Anderson was initially assigned technical duties in the Flight Support Branch of the [Astronaut Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Astronaut_Corps "NASA Astronaut Corps"), but went on to log more than 593 hours in space aboard two Space Shuttle missions.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

### Space Shuttle missions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Space Shuttle missions")]

#### _Endeavour_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Endeavour")]

Main article: [Space Shuttle Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")

Anderson was a mission specialist on [STS-89](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-89 "STS-89")_[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ (January 22–31, 1998), the eighth Shuttle-to-[Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir")[Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_station "Space station") docking mission, during which the crew delivered over 9,000 pounds of scientific equipment, logistical hardware, and water.

In the fifth and last exchange of a U.S. astronaut, STS-89 delivered [Andy Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Thomas "Andy Thomas") to Mir and returned with [David Wolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wolf_(astronaut) "David Wolf (astronaut)"). The mission's duration was 8 days, 19 hours, and 47 seconds, traveling 3.6 million miles in 138 [orbits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbits "Orbits") of the [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:1-3)

#### _Columbia_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Columbia")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Anderson_on_STS-107.jpg/250px-Anderson_on_STS-107.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Anderson_on_STS-107.jpg)

Anderson during the STS-107 mission

Main article: [Space Shuttle Columbia disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster")

STS-107[Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") (January 16–February 1, 2003). Anderson served as [payload commander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payload_Specialist "Payload Specialist") and lieutenant colonel in charge of science experiments on the _Columbia_, NASA's oldest shuttle.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-6) On February 1, 2003, the shuttle was returning to Earth after a successful 16-day trip to orbit, where the crew had conducted more than 80 scientific experiments.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-7)

Unbeknownst to her crew, the orbiter had suffered critical damage during its launch on January 16, when foam from the fuel tank's insulation fell off and tore a hole in _Columbia's_ left wing.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:2-8) During re-entry, the hole allowed super-hot [atmospheric gases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmosphere_of_Earth "Atmosphere of Earth") to penetrate the orbiter's wing, leading to its destruction.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:2-8) The mission's duration was 15 days, 22 hours, and 20 minutes.

Along with the rest of the STS-107 crew, Anderson was killed upon reentry when the shuttle disintegrated over Texas.

The [_Columbia_ Accident Investigation Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Accident_Investigation_Board "Columbia Accident Investigation Board") reported[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-9) that, in addition to the _Columbia_'s physical damage, NASA's management culture was partly responsible for the disaster.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-10)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Anderson had a wife, Sandra Hawkins, and two daughters, Kaycee and Sydney. He also had three sisters.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-11)

Anderson and his family lived in [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston "Houston") at the time of his death, where they attended Grace Community Church.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:3-12) Anderson sang tenor in the church's choir.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:3-12)

## Legacy and tributes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Legacy and tributes")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/MPAndersonMemHwySign.jpg/250px-MPAndersonMemHwySign.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MPAndersonMemHwySign.jpg)

 Sign along [Washington State Route 904](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_State_Route_904 "Washington State Route 904"), commemorating  
Lt. Col. Michael P. Anderson.

*   [State Route 904](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_State_Route_904 "Washington State Route 904"), running through [Cheney, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheney,_Washington "Cheney, Washington"), where Anderson graduated from high school, was renamed in his memory.
*   The science and math wing of Cheney High School is dedicated to his memory.
*   [Asteroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asteroid "Asteroid")[51824 Mikeanderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/51824_Mikeanderson "51824 Mikeanderson") was posthumously named after Anderson.
*   Anderson Hall, in the Columbia Village apartments at the [Florida Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Institute_of_Technology "Florida Institute of Technology") is named after him.
*   Anderson Plaza, the green space in front of the Hixson-Lied Science Center at [Creighton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creighton_University "Creighton University") was named after him in a compromise between the student body, who wanted the Science Center named for Anderson, and the administration who had already sold the naming rights to the Hixson-Lied family.
*   Blair Elementary School on [Fairchild Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairchild_Air_Force_Base "Fairchild Air Force Base") in Washington was renamed Michael Anderson Elementary School in January 2004. Anderson attended the school as a fifth-grader.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-13)
*   Avondale Elementary School in [Avondale, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avondale,_Arizona "Avondale, Arizona") was renamed Michael Anderson Elementary in his honor. Anderson attended school there when he was in the third grade, and one of the school T-shirts was aboard the _Columbia_ on its last voyage.
*   In 2003, Anderson was inducted into the International Forest of Friendship, in Atchison, KS as part of a memorial to the _Columbia_ astronauts.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-14)
*   Anderson Park in [Canton, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton,_Mississippi "Canton, Mississippi") was dedicated in June 2004.
*   An outdoor bronze statue of Anderson was unveiled in [Spokane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spokane,_Washington "Spokane, Washington") in June 2005. Larger-than-life, it was created by local artist Dorothy Fowler, and shows Anderson kneeling with his helmet in one hand and a dove in the other.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-16)
*   A duplicate statue was dedicated at the [Museum of Flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Flight "Museum of Flight") in [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle") in June 2009[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-17) and the museum launched an aerospace program in his honor.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-18)
*   An outdoor mural in the city of Plattsburgh was unveiled in October 2020 honoring Anderson. On July 4, 2021, the city of Plattsburgh held a dedication for the mural, where the Anderson family was given a key to the city and led the annual Independence Day parade.
*   Lunar crater M. Anderson is named after Anderson.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-19)
*   The Creighton University Physics Department, from which Anderson received his master's degree, maintains a statue and physics scholarship in his honor.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-21)

**Michael Phillip Anderson** (December 25, 1959 – February 1, 2003) was a [United States Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force") officer and [NASA astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_astronaut "NASA astronaut"). He and his six fellow crew members were killed in the [Space Shuttle _Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") when the [craft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")[disintegrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In-flight_breakup "In-flight breakup") during its [re-entry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reentry_(orbital) "Reentry (orbital)") into the [Earth's atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_atmosphere "Earth's atmosphere").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:4-1) Anderson served as the payload commander and lieutenant colonel in charge of science experiments on the _Columbia_. He was posthumously awarded the [Congressional Space Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Space_Medal_of_Honor "Congressional Space Medal of Honor").

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Michael Philip Anderson was born in [Plattsburgh, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plattsburgh,_New_York "Plattsburgh, New York") on December 25, 1959, to Barbara and Bobbie Anderson. He was their third child and only son. Bobbie serviced jets at [Plattsburgh Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plattsburgh_Air_Force_Base "Plattsburgh Air Force Base") in Plattsburgh[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) and was transferred to [Fairchild Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairchild_Air_Force_Base "Fairchild Air Force Base"), about 12 miles (19 km) away from [Spokane, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spokane,_Washington "Spokane, Washington"), which Anderson spoke of as his hometown.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:1-3) Anderson graduated from [Cheney High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheney_School_District "Cheney School District") in [Cheney, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheney,_Washington "Cheney, Washington"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-4) one of four [African Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans") in a class of 200 students.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

In 1981, Anderson graduated with a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physics "Physics") and [astronomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomy "Astronomy") from the [University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington") in [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle"). In 1990, he earned a [Master of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") degree in physics from [Creighton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creighton_University "Creighton University") in [Omaha, Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omaha,_Nebraska "Omaha, Nebraska").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-5)

## Air Force career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Air Force career")]

Upon Anderson's graduation from the University of Washington, he was commissioned a [second lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Lieutenant "Second Lieutenant") in the [U.S. Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Air_Force "U.S. Air Force").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) After completing a year of technical training at [Keesler Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keesler_Air_Force_Base "Keesler Air Force Base") in [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi"), Anderson was assigned to [Randolph Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randolph_Air_Force_Base "Randolph Air Force Base") in [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) At Randolph, he served as chief of communication maintenance for the 2015th Communication Squadron and later as director of information system maintenance for the 1920th Information System Group.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

In 1986, Anderson was selected to attend [Undergraduate Pilot Training](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undergraduate_Pilot_Training "Undergraduate Pilot Training") at [Vance Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vance_Air_Force_Base "Vance Air Force Base"), [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) Upon graduation, he was assigned to the [2d Airborne Command and Control Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2d_Airborne_Command_and_Control_Squadron "2d Airborne Command and Control Squadron"), [Offutt Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offutt_Air_Force_Base "Offutt Air Force Base"), [Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebraska "Nebraska") as an [EC-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_EC-135 "Boeing EC-135") pilot, flying the [Strategic Air Command](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_Air_Command "Strategic Air Command")'s airborne command post code-named "[Looking Glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Looking_Glass "Operation Looking Glass")." Anderson completed his master's degree while stationed at Offutt.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

From January 1991 to September 1992, Anderson served as an aircraft commander and [instructor pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_instructor "Flight instructor") in the [920th Air Refueling Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/920th_Air_Refueling_Squadron "920th Air Refueling Squadron"), [Wurtsmith Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wurtsmith_Air_Force_Base "Wurtsmith Air Force Base"), [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan "Michigan").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

From September 1992 to February 1995, Anderson was assigned as an instructor pilot and tactics officer in the [380th Air Refueling Wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/380th_Air_Refueling_Wing "380th Air Refueling Wing"), [Plattsburgh Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plattsburgh_Air_Force_Base "Plattsburgh Air Force Base"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

Anderson logged more than 3,000 hours of flight time when NASA selected him for astronaut training in December 1994.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) Anderson was one of 19 candidates selected from a pool of 2,962 applicants.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

## NASA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: NASA")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Michael_P._Anderson.jpg/250px-Michael_P._Anderson.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Michael_P._Anderson.jpg)

Anderson in 1995

Anderson reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in March 1995.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) He completed a year of training and evaluation, and was qualified for flight crew assignment as a [mission specialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_Specialist "Mission Specialist").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) Anderson was initially assigned technical duties in the Flight Support Branch of the [Astronaut Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Astronaut_Corps "NASA Astronaut Corps"), but went on to log more than 593 hours in space aboard two Space Shuttle missions.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

### Space Shuttle missions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Space Shuttle missions")]

#### _Endeavour_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Endeavour")]

Main article: [Space Shuttle Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")

Anderson was a mission specialist on [STS-89](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-89 "STS-89")_[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ (January 22–31, 1998), the eighth Shuttle-to-[Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir")[Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_station "Space station") docking mission, during which the crew delivered over 9,000 pounds of scientific equipment, logistical hardware, and water.

In the fifth and last exchange of a U.S. astronaut, STS-89 delivered [Andy Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Thomas "Andy Thomas") to Mir and returned with [David Wolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wolf_(astronaut) "David Wolf (astronaut)"). The mission's duration was 8 days, 19 hours, and 47 seconds, traveling 3.6 million miles in 138 [orbits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbits "Orbits") of the [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:1-3)

#### _Columbia_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Columbia")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Anderson_on_STS-107.jpg/250px-Anderson_on_STS-107.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Anderson_on_STS-107.jpg)

Anderson during the STS-107 mission

Main article: [Space Shuttle Columbia disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster")

STS-107[Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") (January 16–February 1, 2003). Anderson served as [payload commander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payload_Specialist "Payload Specialist") and lieutenant colonel in charge of science experiments on the _Columbia_, NASA's oldest shuttle.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-6) On February 1, 2003, the shuttle was returning to Earth after a successful 16-day trip to orbit, where the crew had conducted more than 80 scientific experiments.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-7)

Unbeknownst to her crew, the orbiter had suffered critical damage during its launch on January 16, when foam from the fuel tank's insulation fell off and tore a hole in _Columbia's_ left wing.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:2-8) During re-entry, the hole allowed super-hot [atmospheric gases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmosphere_of_Earth "Atmosphere of Earth") to penetrate the orbiter's wing, leading to its destruction.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:2-8) The mission's duration was 15 days, 22 hours, and 20 minutes.

Along with the rest of the STS-107 crew, Anderson was killed upon reentry when the shuttle disintegrated over Texas.

The [_Columbia_ Accident Investigation Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Accident_Investigation_Board "Columbia Accident Investigation Board") reported[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-9) that, in addition to the _Columbia_'s physical damage, NASA's management culture was partly responsible for the disaster.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-10)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Anderson had a wife, Sandra Hawkins, and two daughters, Kaycee and Sydney. He also had three sisters.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-11)

Anderson and his family lived in [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston "Houston") at the time of his death, where they attended Grace Community Church.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:3-12) Anderson sang tenor in the church's choir.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:3-12)

## Legacy and tributes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Legacy and tributes")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/MPAndersonMemHwySign.jpg/250px-MPAndersonMemHwySign.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MPAndersonMemHwySign.jpg)

 Sign along [Washington State Route 904](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_State_Route_904 "Washington State Route 904"), commemorating  
Lt. Col. Michael P. Anderson.

*   [State Route 904](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_State_Route_904 "Washington State Route 904"), running through [Cheney, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheney,_Washington "Cheney, Washington"), where Anderson graduated from high school, was renamed in his memory.
*   The science and math wing of Cheney High School is dedicated to his memory.
*   [Asteroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asteroid "Asteroid")[51824 Mikeanderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/51824_Mikeanderson "51824 Mikeanderson") was posthumously named after Anderson.
*   Anderson Hall, in the Columbia Village apartments at the [Florida Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Institute_of_Technology "Florida Institute of Technology") is named after him.
*   Anderson Plaza, the green space in front of the Hixson-Lied Science Center at [Creighton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creighton_University "Creighton University") was named after him in a compromise between the student body, who wanted the Science Center named for Anderson, and the administration who had already sold the naming rights to the Hixson-Lied family.
*   Blair Elementary School on [Fairchild Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairchild_Air_Force_Base "Fairchild Air Force Base") in Washington was renamed Michael Anderson Elementary School in January 2004. Anderson attended the school as a fifth-grader.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-13)
*   Avondale Elementary School in [Avondale, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avondale,_Arizona "Avondale, Arizona") was renamed Michael Anderson Elementary in his honor. Anderson attended school there when he was in the third grade, and one of the school T-shirts was aboard the _Columbia_ on its last voyage.
*   In 2003, Anderson was inducted into the International Forest of Friendship, in Atchison, KS as part of a memorial to the _Columbia_ astronauts.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-14)
*   Anderson Park in [Canton, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton,_Mississippi "Canton, Mississippi") was dedicated in June 2004.
*   An outdoor bronze statue of Anderson was unveiled in [Spokane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spokane,_Washington "Spokane, Washington") in June 2005. Larger-than-life, it was created by local artist Dorothy Fowler, and shows Anderson kneeling with his helmet in one hand and a dove in the other.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-16)
*   A duplicate statue was dedicated at the [Museum of Flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Flight "Museum of Flight") in [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle") in June 2009[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-17) and the museum launched an aerospace program in his honor.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-18)
*   An outdoor mural in the city of Plattsburgh was unveiled in October 2020 honoring Anderson. On July 4, 2021, the city of Plattsburgh held a dedication for the mural, where the Anderson family was given a key to the city and led the annual Independence Day parade.
*   Lunar crater M. Anderson is named after Anderson.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-19)
*   The Creighton University Physics Department, from which Anderson received his master's degree, maintains a statue and physics scholarship in his honor.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-21)

# Michael P. Anderson

### Early life and education

Anderson was born in 1959 to Barbara and Bobbie Anderson; his father serviced jets at [Plattsburgh Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plattsburgh_Air_Force_Base "Plattsburgh Air Force Base") in [Plattsburgh, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plattsburgh,_New_York "Plattsburgh, New York").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) Bobbie Anderson was transferred to [Fairchild Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairchild_Air_Force_Base "Fairchild Air Force Base"), about 12 miles away from [Spokane, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spokane,_Washington "Spokane, Washington"), which Anderson spoke of as his hometown.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:1-3) Anderson graduated from [Cheney High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheney_School_District "Cheney School District") in [Cheney, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheney,_Washington "Cheney, Washington"), one of four [African Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans") in a class of 200 students.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

In 1981, Anderson earned a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in physics and astronomy from the [University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington") in [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle"), and in 1990, he was awarded a [Master of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") degree in physics from [Creighton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creighton_University "Creighton University") in [Omaha, Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omaha,_Nebraska "Omaha, Nebraska").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-4)

## Air Force career

Upon Anderson's graduation from the University of Washington, he was commissioned a [second lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Lieutenant "Second Lieutenant") in the [U.S. Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Air_Force "U.S. Air Force").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) After completing a year of technical training at [Keesler Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keesler_Air_Force_Base "Keesler Air Force Base") in [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi"), Anderson was assigned to [Randolph Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randolph_Air_Force_Base "Randolph Air Force Base") in [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) At Randolph he served as chief of communication maintenance for the 2015th Communication Squadron and later as director of information system maintenance for the 1920th Information System Group.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

In 1986, Anderson was selected to attend [Undergraduate Pilot Training](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undergraduate_Pilot_Training "Undergraduate Pilot Training") at [Vance Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vance_Air_Force_Base "Vance Air Force Base"), [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) Upon graduation he was assigned to the [2d Airborne Command and Control Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2d_Airborne_Command_and_Control_Squadron "2d Airborne Command and Control Squadron"), [Offutt Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offutt_Air_Force_Base "Offutt Air Force Base"), [Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebraska "Nebraska") as an [EC-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_EC-135 "Boeing EC-135") pilot, flying the [Strategic Air Command](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_Air_Command "Strategic Air Command")'s airborne command post code-named "[Looking Glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Looking_Glass "Operation Looking Glass")." He completed his master's degree while stationed at Offutt.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

From January 1991 to September 1992, Anderson served as an aircraft commander and [instructor pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_instructor "Flight instructor") in the [920th Air Refueling Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/920th_Air_Refueling_Squadron "920th Air Refueling Squadron"), [Wurtsmith Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wurtsmith_Air_Force_Base "Wurtsmith Air Force Base"), [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan "Michigan").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) From September 1992 to February 1995, he was assigned as an instructor pilot and tactics officer in the [380th Air Refueling Wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/380th_Air_Refueling_Wing "380th Air Refueling Wing"), [Plattsburgh Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plattsburgh_Air_Force_Base "Plattsburgh Air Force Base"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

Anderson had logged more than 3,000 hours of flight time when NASA selected him for astronaut training in December 1994.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) He was one of 19 candidates selected from a pool of 2,962 applicants.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

## NASA

Anderson reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in March 1995.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) He completed a year of training and evaluation, and was qualified for flight crew assignment as a [mission specialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_Specialist "Mission Specialist").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) Anderson was initially assigned technical duties in the Flight Support Branch of the [Astronaut Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Astronaut_Corps "NASA Astronaut Corps"), but went on to log more than 593 hours in space aboard two Space Shuttle missions.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

### Space Shuttle missions

# _Endeavour_

[STS-89](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-89 "STS-89")[_Endeavour_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour") (January 22–31, 1998). Anderson was a mission specialist on STS-89, the eighth Shuttle-to-[Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir")[Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_station "Space station") docking mission, during which the crew delivered more than 9,000 pounds of scientific equipment, logistical hardware, and water.

In the fifth and last exchange of a U.S. astronaut, STS-89 delivered [Andy Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Thomas "Andy Thomas") to Mir and returned with [David Wolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wolf_(astronaut) "David Wolf (astronaut)"). The mission's duration was 8 days, 19 hours, and 47 seconds, traveling 3.6 million miles in 138 [orbits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbits "Orbits") of the [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:1-3)

# _Columbia_

During STS-107, Anderson served as [payload commander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payload_Specialist "Payload Specialist") and lieutenant colonel in charge of science experiments on the [Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia"), NASA's oldest shuttle.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-5) On February 1, 2003, the shuttle was returning to Earth after a successful 16-day trip to orbit, where the crew had conducted more than 80 scientific experiments.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-6)

Unbeknownst to her crew, the orbiter had suffered critical damage during its launch on January 16, when foam from the fuel tank's insulation fell off and tore a hole in _Columbia's_ left wing.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:2-7) During re-entry, the hole allowed super-hot [atmospheric gases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmosphere_of_Earth "Atmosphere of Earth") to penetrate the orbiter's wing, leading to its destruction.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:2-7) The mission's duration was 15 days, 22 hours, and 20 minutes.

The [_Columbia_ Accident Investigation Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Accident_Investigation_Board "Columbia Accident Investigation Board") reported[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-8) that, in addition to the _Columbia_'s physical damage, NASA's management culture was partly responsible for the disaster.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-9)

## Quotes

Prior to the final launch of the _Columbia_, Anderson told reporters: "There's always that unknown."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:4-1)

## Personal life

Anderson was survived by his wife, Sandra Hawkins, and two daughters, Kaycee and Sydney. He was also survived by his parents and three sisters.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-10) Anderson was buried at [Arlington National Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_National_Cemetery "Arlington National Cemetery").

Anderson and his family lived in [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston "Houston") at the time of his death, where they attended [Grace Community Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_Community_Church_(Texas) "Grace Community Church (Texas)").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:3-11) Anderson sang tenor in the church's choir.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:3-11)

Lt. Col. Michael P. Anderson.

*   [Asteroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asteroid "Asteroid")[51824 Mikeanderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/51824_Mikeanderson "51824 Mikeanderson") was posthumously named after Anderson.

*   Anderson Hall, in the Columbia Village apartments at the [Florida Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Institute_of_Technology "Florida Institute of Technology") is named after him.

*   Anderson Plaza, the green space in front of the Hixson-Lied Science Center at [Creighton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creighton_University "Creighton University") was named after him in a compromise between the student body, who wanted the Science Center named for Anderson, and the administration who had already sold the naming rights to the Hixson-Lied family.

*   Blair Elementary School on [Fairchild Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairchild_Air_Force_Base "Fairchild Air Force Base") in Washington was renamed Michael Anderson Elementary School in January 2004. He attended the school as a fifth-grader.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-12)

*   Avondale Elementary School in [Avondale, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avondale,_Arizona "Avondale, Arizona") was renamed Michael Anderson Elementary in his honor. He attended school there when he was in the third grade, and one of the school T-shirts was aboard the _Columbia_ on its last voyage.

*   In 2003, Anderson was inducted into the International Forest of Friendship, in Atchison, KS as part of a memorial to the _Columbia_ astronauts.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-13)

*   Anderson Park in [Canton, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton,_Mississippi "Canton, Mississippi") was dedicated in June 2004.

*   An outdoor bronze statue of Anderson was unveiled in [Spokane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spokane,_Washington "Spokane, Washington") in June 2005. Larger-than-life, it was created by local artist Dorothy Fowler, and shows Anderson kneeling with his helmet in one hand and a dove in the other.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-15)

*   A duplicate statue was dedicated at the [Museum of Flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Flight "Museum of Flight") in [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle") in June 2009[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-16) and the museum launched an aerospace program in his honor.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-17)

*   An outdoor mural in the city of Plattsburgh was unveiled in October 2020 honoring Anderson. On July 4, 2021, the city of Plattsburgh held a dedication for the mural, where the Anderson family was given a key to the city and led the annual Independence Day parade.

*   Lunar crater M. Anderson is named after him.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-18)

*   The Creighton University Physics Department, from which Anderson received his master's degree, maintains a statue and physics scholarship in his honor.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-20)  
Lieutenant Colonel Anderson was an instructor pilot and tactics officer in the U.S. Air Force. Anderson is the recipient of many awards and honors, some of which include the Defense Superior Service Medal, the USAF Meritorious Service Medal and the USAF Achievement Medal with one oak leaf cluster.  
  
Michael Anderson became an astronaut in 1995 and qualified for flight crew assignment as a mission specialist. He flew on Endeavour STS-89, the eighth Shuttle Mir docking mission. He has logged over 593 hours in space.  
  
Anderson served as a mission specialist on [Columbia STS-107](https://www.amfcse.org/columbia). The mission ended abruptly when space shuttle Columbia and its crew perished during entry, 16 minutes before its scheduled landing.  
  
Michael P. Anderson made the ultimate sacrifice and lost his life in service to the national and the space program on February 1, 2003 at 43 years of age.

## About Space Shuttle Columbia

**Space Shuttle _Columbia_** (**OV-102**) was a [Space Shuttle orbiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter "Space Shuttle orbiter") manufactured by [Rockwell International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockwell_International "Rockwell International") and operated by [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA"). Named after the [first American ship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Rediviva "Columbia Rediviva") to circumnavigate the upper North American Pacific coast and the [female personification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_(personification) "Columbia (personification)") of the United States, _Columbia_ was the first of five Space Shuttle orbiters to fly in space, debuting the [Space Shuttle launch vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") on [its maiden flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-1 "STS-1") in April 1981. As only the second full-scale orbiter to be manufactured after the [Approach and Landing Test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approach_and_Landing_Tests "Approach and Landing Tests") vehicle [_Enterprise_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Enterprise "Space Shuttle Enterprise"), _Columbia_ retained unique features indicative of its experimental design compared to later orbiters, such as test instrumentation and distinctive black [chines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chine_(aeronautics) "Chine (aeronautics)"). In addition to a heavier fuselage and the retention of an internal [airlock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airlock "Airlock") throughout its lifetime, these made _Columbia_ the heaviest of the five spacefaring orbiters; around 1,000 kilograms (2,200 pounds) heavier than [_Challenger_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger") and 3,600 kilograms (7,900 pounds) heavier than [_Endeavour_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour"). _Columbia_ also carried [ejection seats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ejection_seat "Ejection seat") based on those from the [SR-71](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird "Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird") during its first six flights until 1983, and from 1986 onwards carried an imaging pod on its [vertical stabilizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertical_stabilizer "Vertical stabilizer").

During its 22 years of operation, _Columbia_ was flown on 28 missions in the [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program"), spending over 300 days in space and completing over 4,000 orbits around Earth. While it was seldom used after completing its objective of testing the Space Shuttle system, and its heavier mass and internal airlock made it less than ideal for planned [Shuttle-Centaur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle-Centaur "Shuttle-Centaur") launches and dockings with [space stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_station "Space station"), it nonetheless proved useful as a workhorse for scientific research in orbit following the [loss of _Challenger_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster") in 1986. _Columbia_ was used for eleven of the fifteen flights of [Spacelab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab "Spacelab") laboratories, all four United States Microgravity Payload missions, and the only flight of [Spacehab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacehab "Spacehab")'s [Research Double Module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_Double_Module "Research Double Module"). The [Extended Duration Orbiter pallet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_Duration_Orbiter#EDO_Pallet "Extended Duration Orbiter") was used by the orbiter in thirteen of the pallet's fourteen flights, which aided lengthy stays in orbit for scientific and technological research missions. _Columbia_ was also used to retrieve the [Long Duration Exposure Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Duration_Exposure_Facility "Long Duration Exposure Facility") and deploy the [_Chandra_ observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandra_X-ray_Observatory "Chandra X-ray Observatory"), and also carried into space the [first female commander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eileen_Collins "Eileen Collins") of an American spaceflight mission, the [first ESA astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulf_Merbold "Ulf Merbold"), the [first female astronaut of Indian origin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla "Kalpana Chawla"), and the [first Israeli astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon "Ilan Ramon").

At the end of its final flight in February 2003, [_Columbia_ disintegrated upon reentry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster"), killing the seven-member crew of STS-107 and destroying most of the scientific payloads aboard. The [_Columbia_ Accident Investigation Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Accident_Investigation_Board "Columbia Accident Investigation Board") convened shortly afterwards concluded that damage sustained to the orbiter's left wing during the launch of STS-107 fatally compromised the vehicle's [thermal protection system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system "Space Shuttle thermal protection system"). The loss of _Columbia_ and its crew led to a refocusing of NASA's human exploration programs and led to the establishment of the [Constellation program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constellation_program "Constellation program") in 2005 and the eventual [retirement of the Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_retirement "Space Shuttle retirement") in 2011. Numerous memorials and dedications were made to honor the crew following the disaster; the [Columbia Memorial Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Memorial_Space_Center "Columbia Memorial Space Center") was opened as a national memorial for the accident, and the [Columbia Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Hills_(Mars) "Columbia Hills (Mars)") in [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars")' [Gusev crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gusev_(Martian_crater) "Gusev (Martian crater)"), which the [_Spirit_ rover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirit_(rover) "Spirit (rover)") explored, were named after the crew. The majority of _Columbia_'s recovered remains are stored at the [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center")'s [Vehicle Assembly Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle_Assembly_Building "Vehicle Assembly Building"), though some pieces are on public display at the nearby [Visitor Complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Visitor_Complex "Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex").
