# Michael P. Anderson

### Early life and education

Anderson was born in 1959 to Barbara and Bobbie Anderson; his father serviced jets at [Plattsburgh Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plattsburgh_Air_Force_Base "Plattsburgh Air Force Base") in [Plattsburgh, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plattsburgh,_New_York "Plattsburgh, New York").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) Bobbie Anderson was transferred to [Fairchild Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairchild_Air_Force_Base "Fairchild Air Force Base"), about 12 miles away from [Spokane, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spokane,_Washington "Spokane, Washington"), which Anderson spoke of as his hometown.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:1-3) Anderson graduated from [Cheney High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheney_School_District "Cheney School District") in [Cheney, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheney,_Washington "Cheney, Washington"), one of four [African Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans") in a class of 200 students.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

In 1981, Anderson earned a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in physics and astronomy from the [University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington") in [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle"), and in 1990, he was awarded a [Master of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") degree in physics from [Creighton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creighton_University "Creighton University") in [Omaha, Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omaha,_Nebraska "Omaha, Nebraska").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-4)

## Air Force career

Upon Anderson's graduation from the University of Washington, he was commissioned a [second lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Lieutenant "Second Lieutenant") in the [U.S. Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Air_Force "U.S. Air Force").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) After completing a year of technical training at [Keesler Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keesler_Air_Force_Base "Keesler Air Force Base") in [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi"), Anderson was assigned to [Randolph Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randolph_Air_Force_Base "Randolph Air Force Base") in [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) At Randolph he served as chief of communication maintenance for the 2015th Communication Squadron and later as director of information system maintenance for the 1920th Information System Group.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

In 1986, Anderson was selected to attend [Undergraduate Pilot Training](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undergraduate_Pilot_Training "Undergraduate Pilot Training") at [Vance Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vance_Air_Force_Base "Vance Air Force Base"), [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) Upon graduation he was assigned to the [2d Airborne Command and Control Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2d_Airborne_Command_and_Control_Squadron "2d Airborne Command and Control Squadron"), [Offutt Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offutt_Air_Force_Base "Offutt Air Force Base"), [Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebraska "Nebraska") as an [EC-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_EC-135 "Boeing EC-135") pilot, flying the [Strategic Air Command](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_Air_Command "Strategic Air Command")'s airborne command post code-named "[Looking Glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Looking_Glass "Operation Looking Glass")." He completed his master's degree while stationed at Offutt.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

From January 1991 to September 1992, Anderson served as an aircraft commander and [instructor pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_instructor "Flight instructor") in the [920th Air Refueling Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/920th_Air_Refueling_Squadron "920th Air Refueling Squadron"), [Wurtsmith Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wurtsmith_Air_Force_Base "Wurtsmith Air Force Base"), [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan "Michigan").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) From September 1992 to February 1995, he was assigned as an instructor pilot and tactics officer in the [380th Air Refueling Wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/380th_Air_Refueling_Wing "380th Air Refueling Wing"), [Plattsburgh Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plattsburgh_Air_Force_Base "Plattsburgh Air Force Base"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

Anderson had logged more than 3,000 hours of flight time when NASA selected him for astronaut training in December 1994.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) He was one of 19 candidates selected from a pool of 2,962 applicants.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

### Special honors[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:1-3)

*   Distinguished graduate, USAF Communication Electronics Officers course

*   The Armed Forces Communication Electronics Associations Academic Excellence Award

*   Undergraduate Pilot Training Academic Achievement Award for Class 87-08 Vance AFB

## NASA

Anderson reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in March 1995.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) He completed a year of training and evaluation, and was qualified for flight crew assignment as a [mission specialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_Specialist "Mission Specialist").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) Anderson was initially assigned technical duties in the Flight Support Branch of the [Astronaut Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Astronaut_Corps "NASA Astronaut Corps"), but went on to log more than 593 hours in space aboard two Space Shuttle missions.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

### Space Shuttle missions

# _Endeavour_

[STS-89](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-89 "STS-89")[_Endeavour_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour") (January 22–31, 1998). Anderson was a mission specialist on STS-89, the eighth Shuttle-to-[Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir")[Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_station "Space station") docking mission, during which the crew delivered more than 9,000 pounds of scientific equipment, logistical hardware, and water.

In the fifth and last exchange of a U.S. astronaut, STS-89 delivered [Andy Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Thomas "Andy Thomas") to Mir and returned with [David Wolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wolf_(astronaut) "David Wolf (astronaut)"). The mission's duration was 8 days, 19 hours, and 47 seconds, traveling 3.6 million miles in 138 [orbits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbits "Orbits") of the [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:1-3)

# _Columbia_

During STS-107, Anderson served as [payload commander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payload_Specialist "Payload Specialist") and lieutenant colonel in charge of science experiments on the [Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia"), NASA's oldest shuttle.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-5) On February 1, 2003, the shuttle was returning to Earth after a successful 16-day trip to orbit, where the crew had conducted more than 80 scientific experiments.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-6)

Unbeknownst to her crew, the orbiter had suffered critical damage during its launch on January 16, when foam from the fuel tank's insulation fell off and tore a hole in _Columbia's_ left wing.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:2-7) During re-entry, the hole allowed super-hot [atmospheric gases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmosphere_of_Earth "Atmosphere of Earth") to penetrate the orbiter's wing, leading to its destruction.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:2-7) The mission's duration was 15 days, 22 hours, and 20 minutes.

The [_Columbia_ Accident Investigation Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Accident_Investigation_Board "Columbia Accident Investigation Board") reported[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-8) that, in addition to the _Columbia_'s physical damage, NASA's management culture was partly responsible for the disaster.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-9)

## Quotes

Prior to the final launch of the _Columbia_, Anderson told reporters: "There's always that unknown."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:4-1)

## Personal life

Anderson was survived by his wife, Sandra Hawkins, and two daughters, Kaycee and Sydney. He was also survived by his parents and three sisters.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-10) Anderson was buried at [Arlington National Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_National_Cemetery "Arlington National Cemetery").

Anderson and his family lived in [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston "Houston") at the time of his death, where they attended [Grace Community Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_Community_Church_(Texas) "Grace Community Church (Texas)").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:3-11) Anderson sang tenor in the church's choir.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:3-11)

## Legacy and tributes

Lt. Col. Michael P. Anderson.

*   [State Route 904](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_State_Route_904 "Washington State Route 904"), running through [Cheney, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheney,_Washington "Cheney, Washington"), where Anderson graduated from high school, was renamed in his memory.

*   The science and math wing of Cheney High School is dedicated to Anderson.

*   [Asteroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asteroid "Asteroid")[51824 Mikeanderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/51824_Mikeanderson "51824 Mikeanderson") was posthumously named after Anderson.

*   Anderson Hall, in the Columbia Village apartments at the [Florida Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Institute_of_Technology "Florida Institute of Technology") is named after him.

*   Anderson Plaza, the green space in front of the Hixson-Lied Science Center at [Creighton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creighton_University "Creighton University") was named after him in a compromise between the student body, who wanted the Science Center named for Anderson, and the administration who had already sold the naming rights to the Hixson-Lied family.

*   Blair Elementary School on [Fairchild Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairchild_Air_Force_Base "Fairchild Air Force Base") in Washington was renamed Michael Anderson Elementary School in January 2004. He attended the school as a fifth-grader.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-12)

*   Avondale Elementary School in [Avondale, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avondale,_Arizona "Avondale, Arizona") was renamed Michael Anderson Elementary in his honor. He attended school there when he was in the third grade, and one of the school T-shirts was aboard the _Columbia_ on its last voyage.

*   In 2003, Anderson was inducted into the International Forest of Friendship, in Atchison, KS as part of a memorial to the _Columbia_ astronauts.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-13)

*   Anderson Park in [Canton, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton,_Mississippi "Canton, Mississippi") was dedicated in June 2004.

*   An outdoor bronze statue of Anderson was unveiled in [Spokane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spokane,_Washington "Spokane, Washington") in June 2005. Larger-than-life, it was created by local artist Dorothy Fowler, and shows Anderson kneeling with his helmet in one hand and a dove in the other.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-15)

*   A duplicate statue was dedicated at the [Museum of Flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Flight "Museum of Flight") in [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle") in June 2009[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-16) and the museum launched an aerospace program in his honor.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-17)

*   An outdoor mural in the city of Plattsburgh was unveiled in October 2020 honoring Anderson. On July 4, 2021, the city of Plattsburgh held a dedication for the mural, where the Anderson family was given a key to the city and led the annual Independence Day parade.

*   Lunar crater M. Anderson is named after him.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-18)

*   The Creighton University Physics Department, from which Anderson received his master's degree, maintains a statue and physics scholarship in his honor.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-20)  
Lieutenant Colonel Anderson was an instructor pilot and tactics officer in the U.S. Air Force. Anderson is the recipient of many awards and honors, some of which include the Defense Superior Service Medal, the USAF Meritorious Service Medal and the USAF Achievement Medal with one oak leaf cluster.  
  
Michael Anderson became an astronaut in 1995 and qualified for flight crew assignment as a mission specialist. He flew on Endeavour STS-89, the eighth Shuttle Mir docking mission. He has logged over 593 hours in space.  
  
Anderson served as a mission specialist on [Columbia STS-107](https://www.amfcse.org/columbia). The mission ended abruptly when space shuttle Columbia and its crew perished during entry, 16 minutes before its scheduled landing.  
  
Michael P. Anderson made the ultimate sacrifice and lost his life in service to the national and the space program on February 1, 2003 at 43 years of age.

## About Space Shuttle Columbia

**Space Shuttle _Columbia_** (**OV-102**) was a [Space Shuttle orbiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter "Space Shuttle orbiter") manufactured by [Rockwell International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockwell_International "Rockwell International") and operated by [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA"). Named after the [first American ship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Rediviva "Columbia Rediviva") to circumnavigate the upper North American Pacific coast and the [female personification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_(personification) "Columbia (personification)") of the United States, _Columbia_ was the first of five Space Shuttle orbiters to fly in space, debuting the [Space Shuttle launch vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") on [its maiden flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-1 "STS-1") in April 1981. As only the second full-scale orbiter to be manufactured after the [Approach and Landing Test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approach_and_Landing_Tests "Approach and Landing Tests") vehicle [_Enterprise_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Enterprise "Space Shuttle Enterprise"), _Columbia_ retained unique features indicative of its experimental design compared to later orbiters, such as test instrumentation and distinctive black [chines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chine_(aeronautics) "Chine (aeronautics)"). In addition to a heavier fuselage and the retention of an internal [airlock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airlock "Airlock") throughout its lifetime, these made _Columbia_ the heaviest of the five spacefaring orbiters; around 1,000 kilograms (2,200 pounds) heavier than [_Challenger_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger") and 3,600 kilograms (7,900 pounds) heavier than [_Endeavour_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour"). _Columbia_ also carried [ejection seats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ejection_seat "Ejection seat") based on those from the [SR-71](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird "Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird") during its first six flights until 1983, and from 1986 onwards carried an imaging pod on its [vertical stabilizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertical_stabilizer "Vertical stabilizer").

During its 22 years of operation, _Columbia_ was flown on 28 missions in the [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program"), spending over 300 days in space and completing over 4,000 orbits around Earth. While it was seldom used after completing its objective of testing the Space Shuttle system, and its heavier mass and internal airlock made it less than ideal for planned [Shuttle-Centaur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle-Centaur "Shuttle-Centaur") launches and dockings with [space stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_station "Space station"), it nonetheless proved useful as a workhorse for scientific research in orbit following the [loss of _Challenger_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster") in 1986. _Columbia_ was used for eleven of the fifteen flights of [Spacelab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab "Spacelab") laboratories, all four United States Microgravity Payload missions, and the only flight of [Spacehab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacehab "Spacehab")'s [Research Double Module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_Double_Module "Research Double Module"). The [Extended Duration Orbiter pallet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_Duration_Orbiter#EDO_Pallet "Extended Duration Orbiter") was used by the orbiter in thirteen of the pallet's fourteen flights, which aided lengthy stays in orbit for scientific and technological research missions. _Columbia_ was also used to retrieve the [Long Duration Exposure Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Duration_Exposure_Facility "Long Duration Exposure Facility") and deploy the [_Chandra_ observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandra_X-ray_Observatory "Chandra X-ray Observatory"), and also carried into space the [first female commander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eileen_Collins "Eileen Collins") of an American spaceflight mission, the [first ESA astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulf_Merbold "Ulf Merbold"), the [first female astronaut of Indian origin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla "Kalpana Chawla"), and the [first Israeli astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon "Ilan Ramon").

At the end of its final flight in February 2003, [_Columbia_ disintegrated upon reentry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster"), killing the seven-member crew of STS-107 and destroying most of the scientific payloads aboard. The [_Columbia_ Accident Investigation Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Accident_Investigation_Board "Columbia Accident Investigation Board") convened shortly afterwards concluded that damage sustained to the orbiter's left wing during the launch of STS-107 fatally compromised the vehicle's [thermal protection system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system "Space Shuttle thermal protection system"). The loss of _Columbia_ and its crew led to a refocusing of NASA's human exploration programs and led to the establishment of the [Constellation program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constellation_program "Constellation program") in 2005 and the eventual [retirement of the Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_retirement "Space Shuttle retirement") in 2011. Numerous memorials and dedications were made to honor the crew following the disaster; the [Columbia Memorial Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Memorial_Space_Center "Columbia Memorial Space Center") was opened as a national memorial for the accident, and the [Columbia Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Hills_(Mars) "Columbia Hills (Mars)") in [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars")' [Gusev crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gusev_(Martian_crater) "Gusev (Martian crater)"), which the [_Spirit_ rover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirit_(rover) "Spirit (rover)") explored, were named after the crew. The majority of _Columbia_'s recovered remains are stored at the [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center")'s [Vehicle Assembly Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle_Assembly_Building "Vehicle Assembly Building"), though some pieces are on public display at the nearby [Visitor Complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Visitor_Complex "Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex").

Biographical Data

Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center

M ICHAEL P. ANDERSON (LIEUTENANT COLONEL,  USAF)
NASA ASTRONAUT (DECEASED)

PERSONAL DATA:  Born December 25, 1959, in Plattsburgh, New York, but
considered Spokane, Washington, to be his hometown.  Died on February 1, 2003 over the
southern United States when Space Shuttle Columbia  and her crew perished during entry,

AWARDS:  Posthumously awarded the Congressional Space Medal of Honor, the NASA
Space Flight Medal, the NASA Distinguished Service Medal, and the Defense
Distinguished Service Medal (DDSM).

SPECIAL HONORS:  Distinguished graduate USAF Communication Electronics Officers course.  Recipient of the Armed Forces
Communication Electronics Associations Academic Excellence Award 1983.  Received the USAF Undergraduate Pilot T raining
Academic Achievement Award for Class 87-08 Vance AFB.  Awarded the Defense Superior Service Medal, the USAF Meritorious
Service Medal, and the USAF Achievement Medal with one oak leaf cluster.

EXPERIENCE:  Anderson graduated form the University of Washington in 1981 and was commissioned a second lieutenant.
After completing a year of technical training at Keesler AFB Mississippi he was assigned to Randolph AFB T exas.  At Randolph he
served as Chief of Communication Maintenance for the 2015 Communication Squadron and later as Director of Information
System Maintenance for the 1920 Information System Group.  In 1986 he was selected to attend Undergraduate Pilot Training at
Vance AFB, Oklahoma. Upon graduation he was assigned to the 2nd Airborne Command and Control Squadron, Offutt AFB
Nebraska as an EC 135 pilot, flying the Strategic Air Commands airborne command post code-named “Looking Glass”.  From
January 1991 to September 1992 he served as an aircraft commander and instructor pilot in the 920th Air Refueling Squadron,
Wurtsmith AFB Michigan.  From September 1992 to February 1995 he was assigned as an instructor pilot and tactics officer in the
380 Air Refueling Wing, P lattsburgh AFB New York.  Anderson logged over 3000 hours in various models  o f the KC-135 and the
T -38A aircraft.

NASA EXPERIENCE:  Selected by NASA in December 1994, Anderson reported to the Johnson Space Center in March 1995.
He completed a year of training and evaluation, and was qualified for flight crew assignment as a mission specialist.  Anderson was
initially assigned technical duties in the Flight Support Branch of the Astronaut Office.  Anderson flew on ST S-89 and STS-107,
logging over 593 hours in space.

SPACE FLIGHT EXPERIENCE:  ST S-  89  Endeavour  (J anuary 22-31, 1998), was the eighth Shuttle  -Mir docking mission during
which the crew transferred more than 9,000 pounds of scientific equipment, logistical hardware and water from the Space Shuttle to
Mir.  In the fifth and last exchange of a U.S. astronaut, ST S-89 delivered Andy Thomas to Mir  and returned with David Wolf.
Mission duration was 8 days, 19 hours and 47 seconds, traveling 3.6 million miles in 138 orbits of the Earth.

ST S-  107  Columbia  (January 16 to February 1, 2003).  T he 16  -day flight was a dedicated science and research mission.  Working
24 hours a day, in two alternating shifts, the crew successfully conducted approximately 80 experiments.  The STS-107 mission
ended abruptly on February 1, 2003 when Space Shuttle Columbia  and the crew perished during entry, 16 minutes before scheduled
landing.  Mission duration was 15 days, 22 hours and 20 minutes.

# Star power Star power Star power

## On the 20th anniversary of the Space Shuttle Columbia tragedy, we remember astronaut Michael Anderson, ’81.

### By Nancy Joseph | December 2022

* * *

*   UW Magazine Facebook
*   [@UWalum](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=On+the+20th+anniversary+of+the+Space+Shuttle+Columbia+tragedy%2C+we+remember+astronaut+Michael+Anderson%2C+%26rsquo%3B81.&url=https%3A%2F%2Fmagazine.washington.edu%2Ffeature%2Fastronaut-michael-anderson-81-had-star-power%2F)
*   [@UWalum](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3A%2F%2Fmagazine.washington.edu%2Ffeature%2Fastronaut-michael-anderson-81-had-star-power%2F&title=Astronaut%20Michael%20Anderson,%20%E2%80%9981,%20had%20star%20power&summary=On+the+20th+anniversary+of+the+Space+Shuttle+Columbia+tragedy%2C+we+remember+astronaut+Michael+Anderson%2C+%26rsquo%3B81.)

* * *

M ichael Anderson was 9 years old when Neil Armstrong stepped onto the moon in 1969. After witnessing that historic moment, Anderson, ’81, was determined to follow in the space pioneer’s footsteps. In a bedroom adorned with model airplanes and rocket ships, he began to memorize NASA astronauts’ names and imagined his name on that list.

Although none of Anderson’s astronaut role models were African American, he was undeterred. “I don’t think I ever thought I _couldn’t_ do it,” he recalled years later. “I never had any serious doubt about it. It was just a matter of when.”

In December 1994, Anderson was selected by NASA to be an astronaut, and in 1998, he realized his dream of going into space, traveling to the Russian space station Mir aboard the Space Shuttle Endeavour. Five years later, he was part of another mission on Space Shuttle Columbia. But he never made it home. The spacecraft disintegrated upon re-entry to Earth on Feb. 1, 2003.

I’d interviewed Anderson after his first shuttle mission for a story about astronauts who hailed from the UW College of Arts & Sciences. His eagerness to return to space had been palpable during the interview. His descriptions of space flight—particularly his own experience of it—were compelling and vivid.

“Right before the engines cut off, you are being pushed back in the seat by 3 Gs of pressure,” he told me, recalling the moment when Endeavour hit orbit about eight minutes into the flight. “Then you suddenly go to zero Gs [zero gravity]. I remember being thrown forward in my seat and then watching everything around me start to float, including ice crystals that had formed outside the vehicle. As the sun caught those ice crystals—thousands of them—they looked like brilliant shining diamonds floating in the darkness of space. But that’s just one of hundreds of moments that stick out in my mind.”

## Destined to soar

![Image 3](https://magazine.washington.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/anderson-columbia375.jpg)
Michael Anderson, left, and the rest of the STS-89 Space Shuttle Endeavour crew take a moment during a Terminal Countdown Demonstration Test.

By age 3, Anderson knew he would venture into space. “It was just the adventure of it,” he later recalled. In an interview with the Spokesman-Review before his first space flight, one of his sisters shared how the future astronaut sent her on imaginary trips to the moon every Saturday morning, beaming her up to the top bunk bed in his room. Not surprisingly, he was hooked on TV shows like “Star Trek” and “Lost in Space.”

The Anderson family moved several times during his childhood, due to his father’s Air Force career. When Anderson, who was born in Plattsburgh, N.Y., was 11, they settled in Cheney, near Spokane. He attended Cheney High School, and years later still thought of Spokane as his hometown.

His next move was to the University of Washington, where he planned to major in aeronautical engineering. However, an elective physics course changed his mind. He was drawn to the elegance of physics, finding it more suited to his interests. He added a second major in astronomy and joined the UW’s Air Force ROTC.

“He was warm, even-keeled, easygoing,” UW friend and classmate William Tyler, ’83, told Columns Magazine in 2003. “There was no stress about him. He was so focused.”

After graduating, Anderson joined the Air Force, first as a communication electronics officer and then as a pilot, aircraft commander, flight instructor and tactics officer. He went on to pursue a master’s degree in physics at Creighton University before joining NASA’s astronaut training program in 1995. By then, there were several African American astronauts, but it remained a small group. (Yvonne Cagle, ’85, was selected as an astronaut in 1996 but never went into space.)

## A UW connection, a Russian rendezvous

![Image 4](https://magazine.washington.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/anderson-dunbar375.jpg)
Bonnie Dunbar and Michael Anderson show their Husky spirit aboard the Endeavour in 1998.

As an astronaut candidate, Anderson began a grueling training program that included survival training, space shuttle simulator exercises, classes in navigation and orbital dynamics, and more. Once he was assigned as mission specialist for Space Shuttle Endeavour, Anderson began one year of mission-specific training with the rest of the crew.

On that crew was another Husky, Bonnie Dunbar, ’71, ’76, who was about to embark on her fifth and final shuttle mission. The pair brought a Husky banner on board to celebrate their UW connection, holding it aloft for cameras as they floated in zero gravity.

“I was always very impressed with him,” Dunbar said of Anderson. “He had a very calm demeanor. He did such a great job on the flight that I recommended him for selection to a future flight.”

The Endeavour crew had multiple goals: to conduct experiments, transfer supplies to space station Mir and deliver an astronaut to Mir while bringing another one home. The work required Russian-American cooperation, which appealed to Anderson. He took Russian language classes in preparation.

“Working with the Russians was one of the highlights of the whole deal,” he said after his return. “It was just fascinating, two countries that had animosity for so long now working together. We can learn a lot from each other. It’s ironic that we have to leave the planet to get along and work together.”

After Endeavour, Anderson was eager to return to space. His opportunity came with a 16-day mission on Space Shuttle Columbia in early 2003. The mission was dedicated to running experiments, ranging from studies of prostate cancer to observing the effects of gravity on harvester ants. Working 24 hours a day in alternating shifts, the crew successfully conducted about 80 experiments in orbit. As the mission’s payload commander, Anderson was responsible for managing the experiments to ensure that everything was done properly.

“This is one of few research flights we’ve had in a long time,” he commented in a video interview for Space.com before the flight. “For someone interested in space science like myself, it’s really the dream flight.”

## Celebrating an extraordinary life

The Columbia mission ended tragically on Feb. 1, 2003, just 16 minutes before the shuttle’s scheduled landing at Cape Canaveral. NASA later confirmed that damage to the spacecraft’s left wing during the launch—damage NASA had mistakenly deemed non-threatening during the mission—allowed hot atmospheric gases to enter the wing upon reentry.

After the disaster, I reread scribbled notes from my interview with Anderson. I had asked him how he handled fear, given the unforgiving nature of space travel. He’d replied that it was never an issue for him.

“I don’t know why that is,” he told me. “Maybe because the training simply prepares you for it. By the time you make it to the actual space flight, you’re so excited. You just want to do your job. Fear has been dealt with. It’s one of those things you simply don’t dwell upon at all.”

And yet Anderson, a husband and father, was not in denial about the risks of his work. At Sunday services two days after the shuttle disaster, Spokane Rev. Freeman Simmons told his congregation about a conversation with Anderson before the flight. As reported in The New York Times, Anderson told the reverend, “If this thing don’t come out right, don’t worry about me. I’m just going on higher.”

Years later, on the 15th anniversary of Anderson’s death, his mother reflected on her son’s legacy. “Even though he had just turned 43, he had a full life,” she told the Spokesman-Review. “He did wonders in that length of time. Sometimes it isn’t the length that you live, it’s the quality.”

To celebrate Anderson’s accomplishments, elementary schools, parks and highways have been renamed in his honor. An asteroid and a lunar crater also bear his name. He was posthumously awarded the Congressional Space Medal of Honor, the NASA Space Flight Medal, the NASA Distinguished Service Medal and the Defense Distinguished Service Medal. A statue of Anderson was unveiled in Spokane’s Riverfront Park in 2005, with a duplicate installed at the Museum of Flight in Seattle, where an aerospace program was created in his honor.

At the UW, the Lt. Col. Michael P. Anderson Memorial Diversity Scholarship was established in 2004. The scholarship encourages underrepresented minority students to pursue the sciences and engineering. To date, 16 students have benefited from the scholarship support.

Anderson would likely be pleased that a scholarship bearing his name supports future scientists and engineers. But that sort of recognition was never his goal.

“The space shuttle program would select people who were more about the program than about themselves, and Mike was very much that kind of person,” said Dunbar. “He wasn’t out there to aggrandize himself, but to really help move human space flight forward. And he did that.”

By age 3, Anderson knew he would venture into space. “It was just the adventure of it,” he later recalled. In an interview with the Spokesman-Review before his first space flight, one of his sisters shared how the future astronaut sent her on imaginary trips to the moon every Saturday morning, beaming her up to the top bunk bed in his room. Not surprisingly, he was hooked on TV shows like “Star Trek” and “Lost in Space.”

The Anderson family moved several times during his childhood, due to his father’s Air Force career. When Anderson, who was born in Plattsburgh, N.Y., was 11, they settled in Cheney, near Spokane. He attended Cheney High School, and years later still thought of Spokane as his hometown.

His next move was to the University of Washington, where he planned to major in aeronautical engineering. However, an elective physics course changed his mind. He was drawn to the elegance of physics, finding it more suited to his interests. He added a second major in astronomy and joined the UW’s Air Force ROTC.

“He was warm, even-keeled, easygoing,” UW friend and classmate William Tyler, ’83, told Columns Magazine in 2003. “There was no stress about him. He was so focused.”

After graduating, Anderson joined the Air Force, first as a communication electronics officer and then as a pilot, aircraft commander, flight instructor and tactics officer. He went on to pursue a master’s degree in physics at Creighton University before joining NASA’s astronaut training program in 1995. By then, there were several African American astronauts, but it remained a small group. (Yvonne Cagle, ’85, was selected as an astronaut in 1996 but never went into space.)

## A UW connection, a Russian rendezvous

![Image 4](https://magazine.washington.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/anderson-dunbar375.jpg)
Bonnie Dunbar and Michael Anderson show their Husky spirit aboard the Endeavour in 1998.

As an astronaut candidate, Anderson began a grueling training program that included survival training, space shuttle simulator exercises, classes in navigation and orbital dynamics, and more. Once he was assigned as mission specialist for Space Shuttle Endeavour, Anderson began one year of mission-specific training with the rest of the crew.

On that crew was another Husky, Bonnie Dunbar, ’71, ’76, who was about to embark on her fifth and final shuttle mission. The pair brought a Husky banner on board to celebrate their UW connection, holding it aloft for cameras as they floated in zero gravity.

“I was always very impressed with him,” Dunbar said of Anderson. “He had a very calm demeanor. He did such a great job on the flight that I recommended him for selection to a future flight.”

The Endeavour crew had multiple goals: to conduct experiments, transfer supplies to space station Mir and deliver an astronaut to Mir while bringing another one home. The work required Russian-American cooperation, which appealed to Anderson. He took Russian language classes in preparation.

“Working with the Russians was one of the highlights of the whole deal,” he said after his return. “It was just fascinating, two countries that had animosity for so long now working together. We can learn a lot from each other. It’s ironic that we have to leave the planet to get along and work together.”

After Endeavour, Anderson was eager to return to space. His opportunity came with a 16-day mission on Space Shuttle Columbia in early 2003. The mission was dedicated to running experiments, ranging from studies of prostate cancer to observing the effects of gravity on harvester ants. Working 24 hours a day in alternating shifts, the crew successfully conducted about 80 experiments in orbit. As the mission’s payload commander, Anderson was responsible for managing the experiments to ensure that everything was done properly.

“This is one of few research flights we’ve had in a long time,” he commented in a video interview for Space.com before the flight. “For someone interested in space science like myself, it’s really the dream flight.”

## Celebrating an extraordinary life

The Columbia mission ended tragically on Feb. 1, 2003, just 16 minutes before the shuttle’s scheduled landing at Cape Canaveral. NASA later confirmed that damage to the spacecraft’s left wing during the launch—damage NASA had mistakenly deemed non-threatening during the mission—allowed hot atmospheric gases to enter the wing upon reentry.

After the disaster, I reread scribbled notes from my interview with Anderson. I had asked him how he handled fear, given the unforgiving nature of space travel. He’d replied that it was never an issue for him.

“I don’t know why that is,” he told me. “Maybe because the training simply prepares you for it. By the time you make it to the actual space flight, you’re so excited. You just want to do your job. Fear has been dealt with. It’s one of those things you simply don’t dwell upon at all.”

And yet Anderson, a husband and father, was not in denial about the risks of his work. At Sunday services two days after the shuttle disaster, Spokane Rev. Freeman Simmons told his congregation about a conversation with Anderson before the flight. As reported in The New York Times, Anderson told the reverend, “If this thing don’t come out right, don’t worry about me. I’m just going on higher.”

Years later, on the 15th anniversary of Anderson’s death, his mother reflected on her son’s legacy. “Even though he had just turned 43, he had a full life,” she told the Spokesman-Review. “He did wonders in that length of time. Sometimes it isn’t the length that you live, it’s the quality.”

To celebrate Anderson’s accomplishments, elementary schools, parks and highways have been renamed in his honor. An asteroid and a lunar crater also bear his name. He was posthumously awarded the Congressional Space Medal of Honor, the NASA Space Flight Medal, the NASA Distinguished Service Medal and the Defense Distinguished Service Medal. A statue of Anderson was unveiled in Spokane’s Riverfront Park in 2005, with a duplicate installed at the Museum of Flight in Seattle, where an aerospace program was created in his honor.

At the UW, the Lt. Col. Michael P. Anderson Memorial Diversity Scholarship was established in 2004. The scholarship encourages underrepresented minority students to pursue the sciences and engineering. To date, 16 students have benefited from the scholarship support.

Anderson would likely be pleased that a scholarship bearing his name supports future scientists and engineers. But that sort of recognition was never his goal.

“The space shuttle program would select people who were more about the program than about themselves, and Mike was very much that kind of person,” said Dunbar. “He wasn’t out there to aggrandize himself, but to really help move human space flight forward. And he did that.”

# African-American astronaut gave ultimate sacrifice during space shuttle mission

[](https://www.af.mil/DesktopModules/ArticleCS/Print.aspx?PortalId=1&ModuleId=850&Article=111653)[](mailto:?Subject=African-American%20astronaut%20gave%20ultimate%20sacrifice%20during%20space%20shuttle%20mission%20-%20Air%20Force&body=Here%20is%20an%20article%20I%20think%20you%20will%20find%20interesting:%20https://www.af.mil/News/Article-Display/Article/111653/african-american-astronaut-gave-ultimate-sacrifice-during-space-shuttle-mission/)

*   Published Feb. 21, 2012

**FORT GEORGE G. MEADE, Md. (AFNS) --**Lt. Col. Michael P. Anderson was one of only a handful of African-American astronauts and was one of the seven crewmembers aboard the Space Shuttle Columbia when it exploded on re-entry just 16 minutes before its scheduled touchdown Feb. 1, 2003. His accomplishments were numerous, and he showed that nothing should get in the way of a person's goals, including their race.   
  
 He was born in December 1959, in Plattsburgh, N.Y., but considered Spokane, Wash., to be his hometown. His interest in and drive for becoming an astronaut started when he was just 2 or 3 years old, according to his father.   
  
 "He made model aircraft from the time he was a small boy until -- well, when he was at NASA, he was still making them," his mother said. "Science and aerospace, those were his things."   
  
 From the shows he watched on television to the classes he later took in school, Anderson always had his sights set on being an astronaut, according to his parents.   
  
 "He set his sights on it, and I think everything he did after that was focusing in that direction, hoping that one day he would get it," his mother said. "And, it worked."   
  
 He received his Bachelor of Science degree in physics/astronomy from the University of Washington in 1981, and also received his commission as a second lieutenant. He received his Master of Science degree in physics from Creighton University in 1990.   
  
 After completing a year of technical training at Keesler Air Force Base, Miss., he was assigned to Randolph AFB, Texas. At Randolph, he served as Chief of Communication Maintenance for the 2015th Communication Squadron and later as Director of Information System Maintenance for the 1920th Information System Group.   
  
 In 1986, he was selected to attend Undergraduate Pilot Training at Vance AFB, Okla. Upon graduation, he was assigned to Offutt AFB, Neb. as an EC 135 pilot, flying Strategic Air Command's airborne command post "Looking Glass."   
  
 From January 1991 to September 1992, he served as an aircraft commander and instructor pilot in the 920th Air Refueling Squadron at Wurtsmith AFB, Mich. From September 1992 to February 1995, he was assigned as an instructor pilot and tactics officer in the 380th Air Refueling Wing in Plattsburgh AFB, N.Y. Anderson logged more than 3,000 hours in various models of the KC-135 and the T-38A aircraft.   
  
 Selected by NASA in December 1994, Anderson reported to the Johnson Space Center in March 1995. He completed a year of training and evaluation, and was qualified for flight crew assignment as a mission specialist. He was initially assigned technical duties in the Flight Support Branch of the Astronaut Office. Anderson flew on STS-89 and STS-107, logging more than 593 hours in space.   
  
 Because of his focus on education, numerous scholarships around the world have been set up in his name, as well as several schools and libraries named after him, including Michael Anderson Elementary at Fairchild AFB, Wash.   
  
 Included in the nation-wide memorials is a life-size statue of Col. Anderson in the middle of Riverfront Park, centered in the town he called home, Spokane. He is outfitted in his space suit and releasing a white dove -- representing peace and humility.   
  
 He was posthumously awarded the Congressional Space Medal of Honor, the NASA Space Flight Medal, the NASA Distinguished Service Medal and the Defense Distinguished Service Medal.

# African-American astronaut gave ultimate sacrifice during space shuttle mission

[](https://www.af.mil/DesktopModules/ArticleCS/Print.aspx?PortalId=1&ModuleId=850&Article=111653)[](mailto:?Subject=African-American%20astronaut%20gave%20ultimate%20sacrifice%20during%20space%20shuttle%20mission%20-%20Air%20Force&body=Here%20is%20an%20article%20I%20think%20you%20will%20find%20interesting:%20https://www.af.mil/News/Article-Display/Article/111653/african-american-astronaut-gave-ultimate-sacrifice-during-space-shuttle-mission/)

*   Published Feb. 21, 2012

**FORT GEORGE G. MEADE, Md. (AFNS) --**Lt. Col. Michael P. Anderson was one of only a handful of African-American astronauts and was one of the seven crewmembers aboard the Space Shuttle Columbia when it exploded on re-entry just 16 minutes before its scheduled touchdown Feb. 1, 2003. His accomplishments were numerous, and he showed that nothing should get in the way of a person's goals, including their race.   
  
 He was born in December 1959, in Plattsburgh, N.Y., but considered Spokane, Wash., to be his hometown. His interest in and drive for becoming an astronaut started when he was just 2 or 3 years old, according to his father.   
  
 "He made model aircraft from the time he was a small boy until -- well, when he was at NASA, he was still making them," his mother said. "Science and aerospace, those were his things."   
  
 From the shows he watched on television to the classes he later took in school, Anderson always had his sights set on being an astronaut, according to his parents.   
  
 "He set his sights on it, and I think everything he did after that was focusing in that direction, hoping that one day he would get it," his mother said. "And, it worked."   
  
 He received his Bachelor of Science degree in physics/astronomy from the University of Washington in 1981, and also received his commission as a second lieutenant. He received his Master of Science degree in physics from Creighton University in 1990.   
  
 After completing a year of technical training at Keesler Air Force Base, Miss., he was assigned to Randolph AFB, Texas. At Randolph, he served as Chief of Communication Maintenance for the 2015th Communication Squadron and later as Director of Information System Maintenance for the 1920th Information System Group.   
  
 In 1986, he was selected to attend Undergraduate Pilot Training at Vance AFB, Okla. Upon graduation, he was assigned to Offutt AFB, Neb. as an EC 135 pilot, flying Strategic Air Command's airborne command post "Looking Glass."   
  
 From January 1991 to September 1992, he served as an aircraft commander and instructor pilot in the 920th Air Refueling Squadron at Wurtsmith AFB, Mich. From September 1992 to February 1995, he was assigned as an instructor pilot and tactics officer in the 380th Air Refueling Wing in Plattsburgh AFB, N.Y. Anderson logged more than 3,000 hours in various models of the KC-135 and the T-38A aircraft.   
  
 Selected by NASA in December 1994, Anderson reported to the Johnson Space Center in March 1995. He completed a year of training and evaluation, and was qualified for flight crew assignment as a mission specialist. He was initially assigned technical duties in the Flight Support Branch of the Astronaut Office. Anderson flew on STS-89 and STS-107, logging more than 593 hours in space.   
  
 Because of his focus on education, numerous scholarships around the world have been set up in his name, as well as several schools and libraries named after him, including Michael Anderson Elementary at Fairchild AFB, Wash.   
  
 Included in the nation-wide memorials is a life-size statue of Col. Anderson in the middle of Riverfront Park, centered in the town he called home, Spokane. He is outfitted in his space suit and releasing a white dove -- representing peace and humility.   
  
 He was posthumously awarded the Congressional Space Medal of Honor, the NASA Space Flight Medal, the NASA Distinguished Service Medal and the Defense Distinguished Service Medal.

## The Black Astronauts

While there are actually quite a few [black astronauts](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2012/02/african_american_astronauts_fs.pdf), two names that immediately come to my mind are [Mae Jemison](https://www.biography.com/people/mae-c-jemison-9542378) and [Ronald E. McNair](https://www.biography.com/people/ronald-mcnair). The [TRIO program](https://www2.ed.gov/about/offices/list/ope/trio/index.html) which led me to my graduate research was actually named after Ronald E. McNair who died during the tragic launch of the [Space Shuttle Challenger STS-51-L](https://www.space.com/18084-space-shuttle-challenger.html).

## Discovering Lieutenant Colonel Michael P. Anderson

Since volunteering at the [David M. Brown Arlington Planetarium](https://www.apsva.us/planetarium-overview/), I’ve become aware another black astronaut, Lieutenant Colonel [Michael P. Anderson](https://history.nasa.gov/columbia/Troxell/Columbia%20Web%20Site/Biographies/Crew%20Profile%20Information/Crew%20Biographies/anderson_biodata.htm). Michael P. Anderson was a member of the crew of the [Space Shuttle Columbia STS-107](https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/shuttle/shuttlemissions/archives/sts-107.html) which disintegrated upon re-entry into the earth’s atmosphere on February 1, 2003. Anderson served as the payload commander in charge of science experiments on the Columbia.

A biography of astronaut [Michael P. Anderson](https://history.nasa.gov/columbia/Troxell/Columbia%20Web%20Site/Biographies/Crew%20Profile%20Information/Crew%20Biographies/anderson_biodata.htm) is readily available on line, but just briefly, he was born into a military family in Plattsburgh, NY but grew up in Spokane, Washington. He earned his Bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the [University of Washington in Seattle](http://www.washington.edu/) in 1981, and in 1990 he was awarded his Master of science degree in physics from [Creighton University](https://www.creighton.edu/). Colonel Anderson entered [NASA](https://www.nasa.gov/) by way of the [United States Airforce](https://www.airforce.com/) where he was selected for astronaut training being one of the 19 candidates selected from 2,962 total applicants. Prior to the STS-107 mission, Anderson participated in the[STS-89 Endeavour](https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/shuttle/shuttlemissions/archives/sts-89.html) mission.

## The Columbia STS-107 Crew

The [Space Shuttle Columbia STS-107](https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/shuttle/shuttlemissions/archives/sts-107.html) disaster occurred due to critical damage to the shuttle’s ‘orbiter’ when foam from the fuel tank’s insulation fell off and tore a hole in Columbia’s left wing. During re-entry, the hole allowed super-hot atmospheric gases to penetrate the orbiter’s wing, leading to its destruction. The other astronauts in the crew included:

• Rick D. Husband  
• William C. McCool  
• Kalpana Chawla  
• David M. Brown  
• Laurel Clark  
• Ilan Ramon

The picture of the [Space Shuttle Columbia STS-107](https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/shuttle/shuttlemissions/archives/sts-107.html) and its crew used in this post was provided by [David M. Brown Arlington Planetarium](https://www.apsva.us/planetarium-overview/).

## The Black Astronauts

While there are actually quite a few [black astronauts](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2012/02/african_american_astronauts_fs.pdf), two names that immediately come to my mind are [Mae Jemison](https://www.biography.com/people/mae-c-jemison-9542378) and [Ronald E. McNair](https://www.biography.com/people/ronald-mcnair). The [TRIO program](https://www2.ed.gov/about/offices/list/ope/trio/index.html) which led me to my graduate research was actually named after Ronald E. McNair who died during the tragic launch of the [Space Shuttle Challenger STS-51-L](https://www.space.com/18084-space-shuttle-challenger.html).

## Discovering Lieutenant Colonel Michael P. Anderson

Since volunteering at the [David M. Brown Arlington Planetarium](https://www.apsva.us/planetarium-overview/), I’ve become aware another black astronaut, Lieutenant Colonel [Michael P. Anderson](https://history.nasa.gov/columbia/Troxell/Columbia%20Web%20Site/Biographies/Crew%20Profile%20Information/Crew%20Biographies/anderson_biodata.htm). Michael P. Anderson was a member of the crew of the [Space Shuttle Columbia STS-107](https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/shuttle/shuttlemissions/archives/sts-107.html) which disintegrated upon re-entry into the earth’s atmosphere on February 1, 2003. Anderson served as the payload commander in charge of science experiments on the Columbia.

A biography of astronaut [Michael P. Anderson](https://history.nasa.gov/columbia/Troxell/Columbia%20Web%20Site/Biographies/Crew%20Profile%20Information/Crew%20Biographies/anderson_biodata.htm) is readily available on line, but just briefly, he was born into a military family in Plattsburgh, NY but grew up in Spokane, Washington. He earned his Bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the [University of Washington in Seattle](http://www.washington.edu/) in 1981, and in 1990 he was awarded his Master of science degree in physics from [Creighton University](https://www.creighton.edu/). Colonel Anderson entered [NASA](https://www.nasa.gov/) by way of the [United States Airforce](https://www.airforce.com/) where he was selected for astronaut training being one of the 19 candidates selected from 2,962 total applicants. Prior to the STS-107 mission, Anderson participated in the[STS-89 Endeavour](https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/shuttle/shuttlemissions/archives/sts-89.html) mission.

## The Columbia STS-107 Crew

The [Space Shuttle Columbia STS-107](https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/shuttle/shuttlemissions/archives/sts-107.html) disaster occurred due to critical damage to the shuttle’s ‘orbiter’ when foam from the fuel tank’s insulation fell off and tore a hole in Columbia’s left wing. During re-entry, the hole allowed super-hot atmospheric gases to penetrate the orbiter’s wing, leading to its destruction. The other astronauts in the crew included:

• Rick D. Husband  
• William C. McCool  
• Kalpana Chawla  
• David M. Brown  
• Laurel Clark  
• Ilan Ramon

The picture of the [Space Shuttle Columbia STS-107](https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/shuttle/shuttlemissions/archives/sts-107.html) and its crew used in this post was provided by [David M. Brown Arlington Planetarium](https://www.apsva.us/planetarium-overview/).

# William C. McCool

> “From our orbital vantage point, we observe an earth without borders, full of peace, beauty and magnificence, and we pray that humanity as a whole can imagine a borderless world as we see it and strive to live as one in peace.”

— William C. McCool

## Early and personal life

McCool was born September 23, 1961, in [San Diego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego "San Diego"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"). His parents divorced when he was young and his mother married Barent McCool, a Naval aviator.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-usnamh-4) McCool was active in the [Boy Scouts of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boy_Scouts_of_America "Boy Scouts of America"), where he became an [Eagle Scout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eagle_Scout_(Boy_Scouts_of_America) "Eagle Scout (Boy Scouts of America)").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-5) His favorite song was "[Imagine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imagine_(John_Lennon_song) "Imagine (John Lennon song)")" by [John Lennon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lennon "John Lennon"), which was played during the STS-107 mission. McCool's favorite band was [Radiohead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiohead "Radiohead"), and the song "[Fake Plastic Trees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fake_Plastic_Trees "Fake Plastic Trees")" was played by [Mission Control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_Control "Mission Control") as a wake-up call.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-6)

McCool died on February 1, 2003, when [Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") broke up over the southern United States during reentry. He was survived by his wife, Lani, and their three sons. McCool is buried in [Anacortes, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anacortes,_Washington "Anacortes, Washington"), where he lived at the time of his death.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NYT-20071205-2)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-7)

## Education

*   1976–77: Attended [John F. Kennedy High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_High_School_(Guam) "John F. Kennedy High School (Guam)"), [Tamuning, Guam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamuning,_Guam "Tamuning, Guam")[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-8)

*   1979: Graduated from [Coronado High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronado_High_School_(Lubbock) "Coronado High School (Lubbock)"), [Lubbock, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lubbock,_Texas "Lubbock, Texas").

*   1983: Received a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [Applied Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Applied_Science "Applied Science") from the [United States Naval Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Naval_Academy "United States Naval Academy").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NYT-20071205-2)

*   1985: Received a [Master of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") degree in [Computer Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_Science "Computer Science") from the [University of Maryland, College Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Maryland,_College_Park "University of Maryland, College Park").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NASA-JSC-1)

*   1991: Graduated from [United States Naval Test Pilot School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Naval_Test_Pilot_School "United States Naval Test Pilot School"), [Naval Air Station Patuxent River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Air_Station_Patuxent_River "Naval Air Station Patuxent River") - Class 101.

*   1992: Received a Master of Science degree in [Aeronautical Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautical_Engineering "Aeronautical Engineering") from the U.S. [Naval Postgraduate School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Postgraduate_School "Naval Postgraduate School").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NASA-JSC-1)

## Flight experience

McCool completed flight training and was designated a [Naval Aviator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Aviator "Naval Aviator") in August 1986. He was assigned to Tactical Electronic Warfare Squadron 129 ([VAQ-129](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VAQ-129 "VAQ-129")) at [NAS Whidbey Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAS_Whidbey_Island "NAS Whidbey Island"), [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state) "Washington (state)"), for initial [EA-6B Prowler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EA-6B_Prowler "EA-6B Prowler") training. McCool's first operational tour was with Tactical Electronic Warfare Squadron 133 ([VAQ-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VAQ-133 "VAQ-133")), where he made two deployments aboard the [aircraft carrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_carrier "Aircraft carrier")[USS _Coral Sea_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Coral_Sea_(CV-43) "USS Coral Sea (CV-43)") to the [Mediterranean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea "Mediterranean Sea") and received designation as a wing-qualified [landing signal officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landing_signal_officer "Landing signal officer") (LSO). In November 1989, McCool was selected for the U.S. Naval Postgraduate School/[Test Pilot School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Naval_Test_Pilot_School "United States Naval Test Pilot School") (TPS) Cooperative Education Program.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NASA-JSC-1)

After graduating from TPS in June 1992, McCool worked as a [TA-4J](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TA-4J "TA-4J") and EA-6B test pilot in Flight Systems Department of Strike Aircraft Test Directorate at [NAS Patuxent River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAS_Patuxent_River "NAS Patuxent River"), [Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland "Maryland"). He was responsible for the management and conduct of a wide variety of projects, ranging from airframe fatigue life studies to numerous avionics upgrades. However, McCool's primary efforts were dedicated to flight test of the [Advanced Capability (ADVCAP) EA-6B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Capability_EA-6B "Advanced Capability EA-6B"). Following his Patuxent River tour, McCool returned to Whidbey Island, and was assigned to Tactical Electronic Warfare Squadron 132 ([VAQ-132](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VAQ-132 "VAQ-132")) aboard the carrier [USS _Enterprise_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Enterprise_(CVN-65) "USS Enterprise (CVN-65)"). He served as Administrative and Operations Officer with the squadron through their work-up cycle, receiving notice of his NASA selection while embarked on _Enterprise_ for her final pre-deployment at sea period.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NASA-JSC-1)

McCool accumulated over 2,800 hours flight experience in 24 aircraft and over 400 carrier arrestments.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-usnamh-4)

## NASA experience

Selected by [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") in April 1996, McCool reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") the following August.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-usnamh-4) He completed two years of training and evaluation, and was qualified for flight assignment as a pilot. Initially assigned to the Computer Support Branch, McCool also served as technical assistant to the director of flight crew operations, and worked Shuttle cockpit upgrade issues for the Astronaut Office.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NASA-JSC-1)

### Spaceflight experience

McCool was pilot of Space Shuttle mission STS-107, January 16 to February 1, 2003, logging 15 days, 22 hours and 20 minutes in space. The 16-day flight was a dedicated science and research mission. Working 24 hours a day, in two alternating shifts, the crew successfully conducted approximately 80 experiments. According to NASA, McCool said of the unique view he and his crewmates had from Columbia:[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-107mem-10)

> From our orbital vantage point, we observe an earth without borders, full of peace, beauty and magnificence, and we pray that humanity as a whole can imagine a borderless world as we see it and strive to live as one in peace.
> 
> 
> — William Cameron McCool, 29 January 2003 onboard _Columbia_

STS-107's mission ended abruptly on February 1, 2003, when _Columbia_ disintegrated during re-entry, 16 minutes before scheduled landing. All seven crew members were killed.

McCool was posthumously awarded the [NASA Space Flight Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Space_Flight_Medal "NASA Space Flight Medal"), the [NASA Distinguished Service Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Distinguished_Service_Medal "NASA Distinguished Service Medal"), the [Defense Distinguished Service Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defense_Distinguished_Service_Medal "Defense Distinguished Service Medal") (DDSM), and the [Congressional Space Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Space_Medal_of_Honor "Congressional Space Medal of Honor").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NASA-JSC-1)

## About Space Shuttle Columbia

**Space Shuttle _Columbia_** (**OV-102**) was a [Space Shuttle orbiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter "Space Shuttle orbiter") manufactured by [Rockwell International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockwell_International "Rockwell International") and operated by [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA"). Named after the [first American ship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Rediviva "Columbia Rediviva") to circumnavigate the upper North American Pacific coast and the [female personification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_(personification) "Columbia (personification)") of the United States, _Columbia_ was the first of five Space Shuttle orbiters to fly in space, debuting the [Space Shuttle launch vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") on [its maiden flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-1 "STS-1") in April 1981. As only the second full-scale orbiter to be manufactured after the [Approach and Landing Test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approach_and_Landing_Tests "Approach and Landing Tests") vehicle [_Enterprise_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Enterprise "Space Shuttle Enterprise"), _Columbia_ retained unique features indicative of its experimental design compared to later orbiters, such as test instrumentation and distinctive black [chines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chine_(aeronautics) "Chine (aeronautics)"). In addition to a heavier fuselage and the retention of an internal [airlock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airlock "Airlock") throughout its lifetime, these made _Columbia_ the heaviest of the five spacefaring orbiters; around 1,000 kilograms (2,200 pounds) heavier than [_Challenger_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger") and 3,600 kilograms (7,900 pounds) heavier than [_Endeavour_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour"). _Columbia_ also carried [ejection seats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ejection_seat "Ejection seat") based on those from the [SR-71](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird "Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird") during its first six flights until 1983, and from 1986 onwards carried an imaging pod on its [vertical stabilizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertical_stabilizer "Vertical stabilizer").

During its 22 years of operation, _Columbia_ was flown on 28 missions in the [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program"), spending over 300 days in space and completing over 4,000 orbits around Earth. While it was seldom used after completing its objective of testing the Space Shuttle system, and its heavier mass and internal airlock made it less than ideal for planned [Shuttle-Centaur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle-Centaur "Shuttle-Centaur") launches and dockings with [space stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_station "Space station"), it nonetheless proved useful as a workhorse for scientific research in orbit following the [loss of _Challenger_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster") in 1986. _Columbia_ was used for eleven of the fifteen flights of [Spacelab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab "Spacelab") laboratories, all four United States Microgravity Payload missions, and the only flight of [Spacehab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacehab "Spacehab")'s [Research Double Module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_Double_Module "Research Double Module"). The [Extended Duration Orbiter pallet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_Duration_Orbiter#EDO_Pallet "Extended Duration Orbiter") was used by the orbiter in thirteen of the pallet's fourteen flights, which aided lengthy stays in orbit for scientific and technological research missions. _Columbia_ was also used to retrieve the [Long Duration Exposure Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Duration_Exposure_Facility "Long Duration Exposure Facility") and deploy the [_Chandra_ observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandra_X-ray_Observatory "Chandra X-ray Observatory"), and also carried into space the [first female commander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eileen_Collins "Eileen Collins") of an American spaceflight mission, the [first ESA astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulf_Merbold "Ulf Merbold"), the [first female astronaut of Indian origin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla "Kalpana Chawla"), and the [first Israeli astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon "Ilan Ramon").

At the end of its final flight in February 2003, [_Columbia_ disintegrated upon reentry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster"), killing the seven-member crew of STS-107 and destroying most of the scientific payloads aboard. The [_Columbia_ Accident Investigation Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Accident_Investigation_Board "Columbia Accident Investigation Board") convened shortly afterwards concluded that damage sustained to the orbiter's left wing during the launch of STS-107 fatally compromised the vehicle's [thermal protection system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system "Space Shuttle thermal protection system"). The loss of _Columbia_ and its crew led to a refocusing of NASA's human exploration programs and led to the establishment of the [Constellation program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constellation_program "Constellation program") in 2005 and the eventual [retirement of the Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_retirement "Space Shuttle retirement") in 2011. Numerous memorials and dedications were made to honor the crew following the disaster; the [Columbia Memorial Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Memorial_Space_Center "Columbia Memorial Space Center") was opened as a national memorial for the accident, and the [Columbia Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Hills_(Mars) "Columbia Hills (Mars)") in [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars")' [Gusev crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gusev_(Martian_crater) "Gusev (Martian crater)"), which the [_Spirit_ rover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirit_(rover) "Spirit (rover)") explored, were named after the crew. The majority of _Columbia_'s recovered remains are stored at the [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center")'s [Vehicle Assembly Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle_Assembly_Building "Vehicle Assembly Building"), though some pieces are on public display at the nearby [Visitor Complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center_Visitor_Complex "Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex").
