**Kalpana Chawla** ([/ˌ k ɑː l p ə n ə ˈ tʃ ɑː v l ə/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); July 1, 1962 – February 1, 2003) was an Indian-American astronaut, [aerospace engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace_engineering "Aerospace engineering"), and pilot. She was the first woman of Indian heritage to fly to space. Chawla participated in two spaceflights, [STS-87](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-87 "STS-87") and STS-107, in 1997 and 2003, respectively. On both of these flights, she conducted scientific experiments researching the effects of [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weightlessness "Weightlessness") on various [physical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physics "Physics") processes. When the crew members in STS-107 descended back to Earth, the [Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") disintegrated due to damage it sustained at liftoff. This killed all seven astronauts on board, including Chawla.

Chawla was born in [Karnal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karnal "Karnal"), Haryana, India, to Banarsi Lal Chawla and Sanjogta Chawla. She had three older siblings: Sunita, Dipa, and Sanjay Chawla. Chawla developed an interest in crewed flight after observing a plane passing over her at the age of three, deciding that she wanted to become an aerospace engineer at the age of 12. She attended Tagore Baal Niketan Senior Secondary School and, after graduating from there, [Dayal Singh College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dyal_Singh_College,_Delhi "Dyal Singh College, Delhi"). Despite receiving opposition from her father, she transferred from the college to take engineering classes at [Punjab Engineering College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punjab_Engineering_College "Punjab Engineering College"), from which she obtained a [Bachelor of Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Engineering "Bachelor of Engineering") (BEng). She then migrated to the United States, where she obtained her [MSc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") from the [University of Texas at Arlington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Arlington "University of Texas at Arlington") (UTA) and her [PhD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Philosophy "Doctor of Philosophy") from the [University of Colorado Boulder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder "University of Colorado Boulder") (CU Boulder). While at CU Boulder, she obtained various [pilot licenses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilot_licensing_and_certification "Pilot licensing and certification"), [instrument ratings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instrument_rating "Instrument rating"), and [flight instructor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_instructor "Flight instructor") certificates. She became a [naturalized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naturalization "Naturalization") US citizen in the early 1990s.

Chawla's professional career began when she was hired to work at [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Ames Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ames_Research_Center "Ames Research Center") in 1988. There, she conducted research into [computational fluid dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_fluid_dynamics "Computational fluid dynamics"). She then joined Overset Methods, Inc., becoming the vice president of the organization in 1993. In 1994, she returned to NASA in the hopes of becoming an astronaut, undergoing a year of training before being assigned as a [mission specialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_specialist "Mission specialist") and [robotic arm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robotic_arm "Robotic arm") operator in her first space mission, STS-87. Her performance in the mission caused some controversy due to the failed deployment of the Shuttle-Pointed Autonomous Research Tool for Astronomy (SPARTAN) module. Her second space mission, STS-107, was both Chawla's and the shuttle _Columbia_'s final mission. When _Columbia_ re-entered into the Earth's atmosphere, hot gases flowed into its broken wing, causing it to disintegrate over Texas and Louisiana 16 minutes before it was due to land at [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center").

Chawla was posthumously awarded the [Congressional Space Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Space_Medal_of_Honor "Congressional Space Medal of Honor"), the [NASA Space Flight Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Space_Flight_Medal "NASA Space Flight Medal"), and the [NASA Distinguished Service Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Distinguished_Service_Medal "NASA Distinguished Service Medal"). Several buildings, spacecraft, and extraterrestrial landmarks have been named in her honor. In addition, numerous documentaries and biographies have been written about both her life and the [_Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") she was in. Over the years, she has become a household name in India because of her ethnicity and achievements, with scholarships and awards being made in her honor, usually to promote female or Indian participation in space exploration.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kalpana_Chawla&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Kalpana Chawla was born on March 17, 1962,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-6) in [Karnal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karnal "Karnal"), Haryana, India. Her father, Banarsi Lal Chawla, was the owner of a tire manufacturing plant. Her mother, Sanjogta Kharbanda, was the daughter of a doctor.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFuruyama2013201-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEncyclopedia.comn.d.-8) Both of her parents were [Punjabi Hindus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punjabi_Hindus "Punjabi Hindus") who were originally from [Gujranwala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gujranwala "Gujranwala") in [West Punjab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Punjab "West Punjab"), having traveled to [East Punjab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Punjab "East Punjab") as refugees during the [Partition of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_of_India "Partition of India") in 1947.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPadmanabhan20038%E2%80%939-9) She had three siblings: sisters Sunita and Dipa and brother Sanjay, of whom she was the youngest.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTECavallaro202350%E2%80%9351-10)

At the time of her birth, Chawla did not have a legal name. Although she was informally called "Montu" by her parents, it was not until she entered school that she chose her own name from a selection of names her parents presented to her.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarveyTillman2022-2)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEInternational_Institute_of_Buffalo2023-11) The name "Kalpana" translates to "idea" or "imagination", which was the reason she chose it.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEInternational_Institute_of_Buffalo2023-11) Relatives and friends often called her "KC", the initials of her first and last name.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarveyTillman2022-2)

As a child, she developed an interest in airplanes after seeing one at the age of three.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarveyTillman2022-2) At the age of 12, she decided that she wanted to become an [aerospace engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace_engineering "Aerospace engineering").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEncyclopedia.comn.d.-8) However, this idea was dismissed by her father, who said that "only guys want to do [aerospace engineering]", instead recommending her to become a doctor or teacher.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChien200649-12) Despite this, she began specializing in science courses such as physics, chemistry, and mathematics at the [Tagore Baal Niketan Senior Secondary School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagore_Baal_Niketan_Sr._Sec._School,_Karnal "Tagore Baal Niketan Sr. Sec. School, Karnal") in Karnal,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEncyclopedia.comn.d.-8) graduating in 1976 "near the top of her class."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTELaunius20083-13)

In 1977, Chawla took a year of pre-university education at Kumari Vidyavati Anand DAV College for Women, also in Karnal.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBritannica2026-14) Afterward, she attended basic engineering courses at [Dayal Singh College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dyal_Singh_College,_Delhi "Dyal Singh College, Delhi").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTECavallaro202352-15) Because there were no engineering colleges in her hometown,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBritannica2026-14) she then moved to [Chandigarh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandigarh "Chandigarh") to attend the aeronautical engineering school at [Punjab Engineering College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punjab_Engineering_College "Punjab Engineering College"), where she studied the principles of theoretical [aerodynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerodynamics "Aerodynamics"), Aircraft Structures, Aircraft Propulsion, Theory of Elasticity, amongst other disciplines, required to obtain a bachelor's degree in Aeronautical Engineering.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPadmanabhan200326-16) She was one of four women in the program and the first female student to take aerospace engineering classes at the college.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones2020-17) However, some professors discouraged her from studying aerospace engineering, suggesting it was not suitable for women and advising her to study courses such as [electrical engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_engineering "Electrical engineering") instead. She graduated from the college in 1982 with a [BEng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Engineering "Bachelor of Engineering").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFuruyama2013201Chien200649-18)

Chawla chose to travel to the US in 1982 to continue her post graduate education and specialization in aerospace.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTELaunius20083-13) She won a scholarship for the college she was interested in, [UTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Arlington "University of Texas at Arlington"), but required her father's permission before being allowed to attend.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEncyclopedia.comn.d.-8) However, she again faced opposition from her father[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTELaunius20083-13) until he learned more about her accomplishments and aspirations, after which he acquiesced and helped her obtain an American [visa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travel_visa "Travel visa") to study at UTA.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEncyclopedia.comn.d.-8) She earned her [MSc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") from the university in 1984 with the [thesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thesis "Thesis")_Optimization of cross flow fan housing for airplane wing installation_.[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-20)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUTAn.d.Chawla1984-21) She also met her husband, pilot Jean-Pierre Harrison, while at the school, and the two married on December 2, 1983.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones2020-17)

Chawla then attended [CU Boulder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado_Boulder "University of Colorado Boulder"), where she first decided that she wanted to join the space program, receiving her PhD in 1988 with the thesis _Computation of dynamics and control of unsteady vortical flows_.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChawla1988Chien200650Furuyama2013201-22) While attending CU Boulder, Chawla began taking flying lessons at the [Boulder Municipal Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boulder_Municipal_Airport "Boulder Municipal Airport"), eventually receiving commercial [pilot licenses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilot_licensing_and_certification "Pilot licensing and certification") permitting her to fly various types of [land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airplane "Airplane") and [seaplanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seaplane "Seaplane"), as well as [gliders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glider_(sailplane) "Glider (sailplane)").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarrison201146Cavallaro202353-23) She also received [instrument ratings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instrument_rating "Instrument rating") for airplanes[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTENASA2004-1) and later became certified as a [flight instructor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_instructor "Flight instructor") for single-engine airplanes and [flight instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_instruments "Flight instruments").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarrison201155-24)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kalpana_Chawla&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### NASA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kalpana_Chawla&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: NASA")]

[![Image 8: Chawla and her husband posing for a picture.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Kalpana_Chawla_and_husband.jpg/250px-Kalpana_Chawla_and_husband.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kalpana_Chawla_and_husband.jpg)

Chawla and her husband before the launch of STS-87.

In 1988, Chawla began working at [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Ames Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ames_Research_Center "Ames Research Center"), where she initially conducted [computational fluid dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_fluid_dynamics "Computational fluid dynamics") research on [vertical and/or short take-off and landing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V/STOL "V/STOL") (V/STOL) concepts. Her research there mostly focused on the simulation of [air flow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airflow "Airflow") around aircraft such as the [Harrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrier_jump_jet "Harrier jump jet"), with particular focus on the [ground effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ground_effect_(aerodynamics) "Ground effect (aerodynamics)").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTENASA2004-1) She subsequently studied how to use multiple computers to solve [fluid flow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluid_dynamics "Fluid dynamics") problems, testing these methods by calculating [powered lift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Powered_lift "Powered lift") effects.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTENASA2004Launius20083Furuyama2013201-25) Sometime in the early 1990s, she became a [naturalized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naturalization "Naturalization") US citizen, a requirement for becoming a NASA astronaut.[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-27)

Chawla joined Overset Methods, Inc., a non-profit research organization based in [Los Altos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Altos,_California "Los Altos, California"), California, as both a research scientist and the organization's vice president in 1993.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTELaunius20083Furuyama2013201Jones2020-28) Her work focused on simulating problems involving multiple moving objects and designing techniques to support [aerodynamic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerodynamics "Aerodynamics") optimization.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTENASA2004-1) While in Los Altos, she joined the West Valley Flying Club at the [Palo Alto Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palo_Alto_Airport "Palo Alto Airport") and learned [Bharatanatyam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharatanatyam "Bharatanatyam") from the Abhinaya Dance Company in [San Jose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Jose,_California "San Jose, California").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPadmanabhan200343%E2%80%9346-29) In December 1994, she returned to NASA to undergo training as a candidate astronaut at the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") as part of [NASA Astronaut Group 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Astronaut_Group_15 "NASA Astronaut Group 15"). As part of this training, she attended classes in various sciences relevant to spaceflight, such as [space medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_medicine "Space medicine"), [planetary science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_science "Planetary science"), and [materials science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materials_science "Materials science"). She was also required to take classes teaching skills ranging from flying certain aircraft to [parasail flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parasailing "Parasailing") and [scuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_skills "Scuba skills").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrespo2024-30)

Eventually, she was eligible to work on technical assignments in office settings, which led up to assignments as a crew member in space shuttles.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrespo2024-30) In 1995, she was assigned to the [extravehicular activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extravehicular_activity "Extravehicular activity") and [robotics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robotics "Robotics") divisions of the [NASA Astronaut Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Astronaut_Corps "NASA Astronaut Corps"). In the corps, she was made a crew representative to work on the technical issues that would arise in NASA's robotics. Most of her working time was spent in the [Shuttle Avionics Integration Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Avionics_Integration_Laboratory "Shuttle Avionics Integration Laboratory"), where she developed Robotic Situational Awareness Displays and test space shuttle control software.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTENASA2004-1)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHessCampionHerring1994ShaylerMoule2005282Launius20083Jones2020-31)

### First space mission

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kalpana_Chawla&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: First space mission")]

Main article: [STS-87](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-87 "STS-87")

[![Image 9: The crew of STS-87 posing for a picture.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Sts-87_crew.jpg/250px-Sts-87_crew.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sts-87_crew.jpg)

The crew of STS-87 in September 1997. From left to right, in orange: Chawla, [Lindsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Lindsey "Steven Lindsey"), [Kregel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_R._Kregel "Kevin R. Kregel"), [Kadeniuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonid_Kadeniuk "Leonid Kadeniuk"); in white: [Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_E._Scott "Winston E. Scott"), [Doi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takao_Doi "Takao Doi").

Chawla's first space mission began on November 19, 1997, as part of the six-astronaut crew that flew on the [Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") flight [STS-87](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-87 "STS-87").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTENASA2004-1) It was the fourth flight to hold the US Microgravity Payload (USMP-4) and [Spartan 201](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spartan_201 "Spartan 201") module,[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTESTS-87n.d.-32) two of its [payloads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payload "Payload") with which to conduct experiments on [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weightlessness "Weightlessness") and the [Sun's outer atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stellar_corona "Stellar corona"), respectively.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTESSM_STS-87n.d.5%E2%80%936-33) In the mission, Chawla served as a [mission specialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_specialist "Mission specialist"), [robotic arm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robotic_arm "Robotic arm") operator,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTENASA2004-1) and backup [flight engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_engineer "Flight engineer") during liftoff. After STS-87 launched, Chawla became the first woman of Indian origin to go to space; [Inder Kumar Gujral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inder_Kumar_Gujral "Inder Kumar Gujral"), the then prime minister of India, called her to congratulate her on her flight, expressing pride on behalf of the people of India and lauding Chawla for inspiring Indian women and children.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones2020-17)

Chawla supervised and performed experiments in STS-87. As part of the mission, Chawla studied how to mix liquids evenly to create specific metal combinations that could be used in future computer chips. Using _Columbia_'s Middeck Glovebox, she worked with [immiscibles](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/immiscible "wiktionary:immiscible") to understand the causes behind their separation.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans2005333%E2%80%93335-34)

Chawla was assigned to deploy the SPARTAN during the mission. Due to a power surge that damaged its control system, the SPARTAN failed to perform its expected pirouette movement minutes after she had deployed it. Chawla attempted to grapple the satellite with the shuttle's robotic arm but did not receive a clear signal on the control panel showing it was secured, causing her to move the arm back. In the process, she accidentally hit the SPARTAN, making it spin at two degrees per second. Fellow astronaut [Kevin R. Kregel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_R._Kregel "Kevin R. Kregel") also attempted to grapple the payload by matching its spin with the shuttle's, but this movement was ultimately aborted. In the end, astronauts [Winston E. Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_E._Scott "Winston E. Scott") and [Takao Doi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takao_Doi "Takao Doi") performed a spacewalk to retrieve the payload.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans2005320%E2%80%93327-35)

[![Image 10: The SPARTAN module in the backdrop of the Earth's oceans.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/Sts087-706-020.jpg/250px-Sts087-706-020.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sts087-706-020.jpg)

The deployment of the SPARTAN module.

Some members of the press criticized Chawla for her handling of the SPARTAN payload, but Kregel refused to assign blame in an interview with the _[Orlando Sentinel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlando\_Sentinel "Orlando Sentinel")_:

> We'd be very foolish if we tried to second-guess or tried to figure out what the actual turn of events were without having all the information... We're six folks up here; we know what happened on our side, we'll get together with the folks on the ground and we'll put the whole story together and make sure it never happens again. Sure, we're always a bit disappointed if we don't get the full mission accomplished, but we did retrieve the satellite, and so the important thing is we're bringing Spartan back down to Earth, and it'll get to fly another day.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans2005338-36)

NASA formed a team to investigate the deployment failure on December 4, 1997. The investigation initially attributed the failure to "crew error", but Chawla was ultimately exonerated, with the investigators citing insufficient training, errors in software interfaces, and poor communication with [ground control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_control_center "Mission control center") as the causes of the incident.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFurniss1998Evans2005338%E2%80%93340-37) In all, by the end of the STS-87 mission on December 5, 1997, Chawla traveled 10.4 million miles in 252 orbits of the Earth, logging more than 376 hours (15 days and 16 hours) in space.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTENASA2004-1)

Chawla's spaceflight was widely reported around the world. She became especially well-known in India,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTESethulekshmi2022-38) with an image of her taken while she was in the shuttle being used as a cover image for India's _[The Week](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Week\_(Indian\_magazine) "The Week (Indian magazine)")_,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEncyclopedia.comn.d.-8) an Indian news magazine and one of the largest published in English.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMRUC2014-39) In an interview with the [New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times"), the head of the Washington office of the [Indian Space Research Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISRO "ISRO"), India's correspondent to NASA, said that "After her first flight, she became a national hero."[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPolgreen2003-40)

After the mission, in January 1998, Chawla was assigned to be a crew representative for [shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") and [station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_station "Space station") flight crew equipment.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTENASA2004-1) She was given a technical assignment advising shuttle engineers on different aspects of payload development and the astronaut experience.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChien200656-41) Soon after, she was selected to head the Astronaut Corps's Crew Systems and Habitability department.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPadmanabhan200379-42)

### Second space mission and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kalpana_Chawla&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Second space mission and death")]

Main articles: STS-107 and [Space Shuttle Columbia disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster")

[![Image 11: The crew of STS-107 posing for a picture.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/Crew_of_STS-107%2C_official_photo.jpg/250px-Crew_of_STS-107%2C_official_photo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Crew_of_STS-107,_official_photo.jpg)

The crew of STS-107 in October 2001. From left to right: [Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown "David M. Brown"), Husband, [Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark "Laurel Clark"), Chawla, Anderson, McCool, and [Ramon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon "Ilan Ramon").

On July 27, 2000, Chawla was selected for her second flight as part of the crew of STS-107.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChien200690-43) STS-107 was delayed 13 times over two years for a variety of reasons, including [orbiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter "Space Shuttle orbiter") maintenance and the discovery of cracks in the shuttle engine flow liners on July 19, 2002. The mission finally launched on January 16, 2003.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGehman_Jr._et_al.200328-44) As the mission's [flight engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_engineer "Flight engineer"), she provided assistance to pilot William C. McCool during liftoff.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGehman_Jr._et_al.200329Chien2006124-45)

STS-107 was a multidisciplinary scientific mission modeled after the previous [STS-90](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-90 "STS-90").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGehman_Jr._et_al.200327-46) The crew was assigned to two teams working in shifts to ensure that experiments were conducted nonstop. Chawla worked on the Red Team alongside fellow astronauts [Ilan Ramon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon "Ilan Ramon"), [Laurel Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark "Laurel Clark"), and Rick Husband.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans2005414Chien2006168-47) She performed a variety of experiments while in orbit, researching [astroculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_farming "Space farming")[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGehman_Jr._et_al.200329Evans2005421%E2%80%93422Chien2006158%E2%80%93159-48) and the effects of low gravity[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYangZahnMerchant2023-49) on the properties of [combustion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combustion "Combustion"), [crystal growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_growth "Crystal growth"),[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGehman_Jr._et_al.200329Evans2005421%E2%80%93422Chien2006158%E2%80%93159-48) cancer growth,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYangZahnMerchant2023-49)[granular materials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granular_material "Granular material"), and [mist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mist "Mist").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGehman_Jr._et_al.200329Evans2005421%E2%80%93422Chien2006158%E2%80%93159-48) Other experiments included those to recycle water on the International Space Station, study the Sun, and analyze the behavior of insects and fish in space, the latter having been tested on behalf of the elementary students that created them.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarveyTillman2022-2) Overall, the crew of STS-107 performed over 80 experiments in various disciplines.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTENASA2004Evans2005419%E2%80%93424-50)

As the flight engineer, Chawla was tasked, alongside mission specialist Clark, with assessing the shuttle's system before [re-entry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_entry "Atmospheric entry") on February 1.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans2005426%E2%80%93427-51)_[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_ began re-entry at 8:44 a.m. on February 1. At 8:54 a.m, four sensors on the shuttle's wing failed, and at 9:00 a.m, the shuttle began disintegrating in the sky above Texas and Louisiana, killing all seven crew members aboard 16 minutes before they were due to land at the [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") in Florida.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTENASA2004-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarveyTillman2022-2)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYangZahnMerchant2023-49)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGehman_Jr._et_al.200338%E2%80%9339Jones2020-52) Following the incident, both [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") and various independent groups began investigating the cause of the disaster.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarveyTillman2022-2) For the next two years, NASA suspended all space flights while investigations were ongoing.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYangZahnMerchant2023-49) In 2003, a report by the [_Columbia_ Accident Investigation Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Accident_Investigation_Board "Columbia Accident Investigation Board") found that a piece of [insulating foam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyurethane_foam "Polyurethane foam") broke off from the shuttle's [external tank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_external_tank "Space Shuttle external tank") during liftoff, striking the left wing of the orbiter.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGehman_Jr._et_al.2003138-53) When _Columbia_ began re-entry, hot gases entered the damaged wing, leading to the shuttle's destruction.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChien2006vii-54)

NASA established a team near [Hemphill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hemphill,_Texas "Hemphill, Texas"), Texas, to search for the remains of the crew.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeinbachWard202097-55) On February 4 or 5, NASA began transporting the recovered remains to the [Armed Forces Institute of Pathology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armed_Forces_Institute_of_Pathology "Armed Forces Institute of Pathology") at [Dover Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dover_Air_Force_Base "Dover Air Force Base").[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-57)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChien2006372LeinbachWard2020117-56) By February 11, all crew members' remains had been recovered, including Chawla's. A memorial service was held in Hemphill that afternoon.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeinbachWard2020131%E2%80%93132-58) Chawla's remains were ultimately cremated and scattered at [Zion National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zion_National_Park "Zion National Park").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChien2006372-59) Considering both her flight in STS-87 and STS-107, she logged a total of 30 days, 14 hours, and 54 minutes in space by the end of her career.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTENASA2004-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarveyTillman2022-2)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kalpana_Chawla&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Legacy")]

Chawla was the recipient of numerous posthumous honors. On February 3, 2003, it was announced that the girls' hostel at Punjab Engineering College, where Chawla obtained her [BEng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Engineering "Bachelor of Engineering"), would be named after her. A prize consisting of [INR₹](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_rupee "Indian rupee")25,000, a medal, and a certificate was also created to reward the top students in the [aeronautical engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace_engineering "Aerospace engineering") department.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Indian_Express''2003-60) Also in February, the then prime minister of India, [Atal Bihari Vajpayee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atal_Bihari_Vajpayee "Atal Bihari Vajpayee"), announced that the satellite MetSat-1 would be renamed to "[Kalpana-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana-1 "Kalpana-1")".[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMOSDACn.d.-61) Then, in August, the asteroid [51826 Kalpanachawla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/51826_Kalpanachawla "51826 Kalpanachawla") was named after her, one of seven asteroids named after the _Columbia'_ s crew.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUri2023-62) The [Florida Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Institute_of_Technology "Florida Institute of Technology") named one of its residence buildings after Chawla in 2003 as part of "Columbia Village", which was dedicated to the seven _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_ astronauts.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Florida_Tech_News''2003-63)[Steve Morse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Morse "Steve Morse") of the band [Deep Purple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Purple "Deep Purple") released the song "Contact Lost" in 2003 in memory of the [_Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster").[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''UPI''2003-64)

[![Image 12: Refer to the caption.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Kalpana_Chawla_Hall_Univ_Texas_Arlington.JPG/250px-Kalpana_Chawla_Hall_Univ_Texas_Arlington.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kalpana_Chawla_Hall_Univ_Texas_Arlington.JPG)

Kalpana Chawla Hall, [University of Texas at Arlington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Arlington "University of Texas at Arlington").

In 2003, 74th Street in [Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens "Queens"), New York City, was named "Kalpana Chawla Way" after her.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTETimes_of_India2003-65)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrownstoner2013-66) Another street, Kalpana Chawla Street, was also named after her, located in [Coimbatore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coimbatore "Coimbatore"), Tamil Nadu, India.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAshsan2023-67) The following year, [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") named a [supercomputer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercomputer "Supercomputer") after her, [Kalpana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_(supercomputer) "Kalpana (supercomputer)").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMewhinney2004-68) Also in 2004, the [Indian Institute of Technology, Kharagpur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IIT_Kharagpur "IIT Kharagpur"), named the Kalpana Chawla Space Technology Cell after her.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEIndian_Institute_of_Technologyn.d.-69) Seven peaks in the [Columbia Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Hills_(Mars) "Columbia Hills (Mars)") on Mars were named after the _Columbia_ astronauts on February 2, 2004, with one of them being named after Chawla.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGarber2013-70) Two days later, on February 4, Chawla was posthumously awarded the [Congressional Space Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Space_Medal_of_Honor "Congressional Space Medal of Honor") by President [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTENASA2023-71) She was also awarded the [NASA Space Flight Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Space_Flight_Medal "NASA Space Flight Medal") and the [NASA Distinguished Service Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Distinguished_Service_Medal "NASA Distinguished Service Medal").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTENASA2004-1) In March, the [Government of Karnataka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Karnataka "Government of Karnataka") instituted the "Kalpana Chawla Award" to recognize young female scientists.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Hindu''2004-72) Then, in September, [UTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Arlington "University of Texas at Arlington"), where Chawla obtained her [MSc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") in 1984, opened "Kalpana Chawla Hall", also called "KC Hall".[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWong2004-73) The lunar crater "Chawla" was named after her in 2006.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUSGS2010Uri2023-74) The Kalpana Chawla Planetarium in [Haryana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haryana "Haryana") was also dedicated to her in 2007.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaryana_Governmentn.d.-75) Novelist [Peter David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_David "Peter David") named a shuttlecraft, the _Chawla_, after her in his 2007 [Star Trek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek "Star Trek") novel, _Star Trek: The Next Generation: Before Dishonor_.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavid200724-76)

In 2010, a memorial display was dedicated to Chawla in UTA's [Nedderman Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nedderman_Hall "Nedderman Hall").[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUTAn.d.-77) That same year, the Kalpana Chawla ISU Scholarship was founded to support Indian women in space education.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEIN_Presswire2024-78) In 2011, Chalwa's husband published a biography on her titled _The Edge of Time_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarveyTillman2022-2) In 2017, the [Kalpana Chawla Government Medical College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla_Government_Medical_College "Kalpana Chawla Government Medical College") was established in [Karnal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karnal "Karnal").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGupta2023-79) Then, in 2020, she became the focus of the second season of the [National Geographic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Geographic "National Geographic") documentary series _Mega Icons_ alongside musician [A. R. Rahman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._R._Rahman "A. R. Rahman"), actress [Deepika Padukone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deepika_Padukone "Deepika Padukone"), and industrialist [Ratan Tata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratan_Tata "Ratan Tata").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Indian_Express''2020-80) The [fourteenth contracted Northrop Grumman Cygnus spacecraft mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cygnus_NG-14 "Cygnus NG-14"), which was launched in October 2020 to deliver supplies to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"), was named the S.S. _Kalpana Chawla_ in her honor.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPearlman2020Gohd2020-81) On April 1, 2022, a satellite nicknamed after Chawla was launched into space: [ÑuSat 24, COSPAR 2022-033X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%91uSat#List_of_satellites "ÑuSat").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChristiaens2023-82) Finally, a fictionalized version of Chawla appears in the 2023 movie _[A Million Miles Away](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Million\_Miles\_Away\_(film) "A Million Miles Away (film)")_, where she is played by actress [Sarayu Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarayu_Rao "Sarayu Rao").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalpana_Chawla#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_Le%C3%B3n2023-83)
