The unstable craft rolled and bucked, pitching the astronauts about. Less than a minute passed before the ship depressurized, [killing the crew](https://www.space.com/6267-report-columbia-astronauts-killed-seconds.html). Also on board were Rick Husband, Laurel Clark, Ilan Ramon, David Brown, William McCool and Michael Anderson.

The shuttle broke up over Texas and Louisiana before plunging into the ground. The accident was the second major disaster for the space shuttle program, following the 1986 explosion of the shuttle [Challenger](https://www.space.com/18084-space-shuttle-challenger.html).

**Related**: [Debris from space shuttle Columbia disaster found in Texas](https://www.space.com/12518-space-shuttle-columbia-debris-texas.html)

NASA and independent groups both investigated the Columbia disaster in hopes of preventing another such tragedy. Examples include the [Columbia Accident Investigation Board](https://www.space.com/19476-space-shuttle-columbia-disaster-oversight.html) (2003) and NASA's [Columbia Crew Survival Investigation Report](https://www.space.com/6268-columbia-accident-report-astronaut-safety.html) (released in 2008).

Each year, NASA marks the loss of the Columbia crew, as well as the crews of the Challenger space shuttle and Apollo 1, on the last Thursday of January; the fatal missions are also regularly referenced when NASA personnel discuss the importance of prioritizing safety in human spaceflight.

No NASA mission has been fatal since the Columbia disaster.


### Chawla's legacy

Shortly after the Columbia disaster, [scientists named](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/asteroids-dedicated-to-space-shuttle-columbia-crew) seven asteroids after each crewmember as a "celestial memorial." To mark the first anniversary of the disaster, NASA also [named seven hills](https://www.nasa.gov/home/hqnews/2004/feb/HQ_04048_columbia_landmarks.html) on Mars for the lost crew.

The University of Texas [dedicated a Kalpana Chawla memorial](http://www.collectspace.com/ubb/Forum41/HTML/000331.html) at the Arlington College of Engineering in 2010. At the time of its opening, the display included a flight suit, photographs, information about Chawla's life, and a flag that was flown over the Johnson Space Center during a memorial for the Columbia astronauts.

In October 2020, a commercial cargo spacecraft named after Chawla launched to the [International Space Station](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/missions/international-space-station) (ISS). Northrop Grumman’s Cygnus capsule was named the S.S. Kalpana Chawla, as it is the company’s policy to dedicate their Cygnus capsules to someone who has played a pivotal role in human spaceflight.

"Chawla was selected in honor of her prominent place in history as the first woman of Indian descent to go to space," Northrop Grumman officials [wrote in a statement](https://www.northropgrumman.com/space/cygnus-ng-14-mission-page/).


### Additional resources and reading

Chawla's widower, Jean-Pierre Harrison, wrote a biography called "[The Edge of Time](https://target.georiot.com/Proxy.ashx?tsid=72128&GR_URL=https%3A%2F%2Famazon.com%2FEdge-Time-Authoritative-Biography-Kalpana-ebook%2Fdp%2FB0063LCWGA%3Ftag%3Dftr-space-us-20%26ascsubtag%3Dhawk-custom-tracking-20)," which he published in 2011. In addition, several documentaries have been produced about the Columbia crew, including "[Astronaut Diaries: Remembering the Columbia Shuttle Crew](https://www.space.com/1072-documentary-intimate-columbia-crew.html)" (2005), and one that focused on astronaut Ilan Ramon, called "[Space Shuttle Columbia: Mission of Hope](https://www.space.com/19539-columbia-shuttle-astronaut-holocaust-scroll-film.html)" (2013).

Kalpana Chawla was the first Indian-American woman to go to space.  
  
Chawla began working at the NASA Ames Research Center in 1988. After becoming a naturalized citizen in 1991, she applied for the NASA Astronaut Corps and was selected in 1994 as an astronaut candidate. Chawla was assigned as mission specialist and prime robotic arm operator on STS-87 and when the mission launched in 1997 on Space Shuttle Columbia, she became the first Indian-born woman in space. She flew on Columbia again on STS-107 in 2003, which ended tragically when Space Shuttle Columbia broke apart during reentry. In total, Chawla logged 30 days, 14 hours and 54 minutes in space. She was posthumously awarded the Congressional Space Medal of Honor, the NASA Space Flight Medal, and the NASA Distinguished Service Medal. **Kalpana Chawla** (born March 17, 1962, [Karnal](https://www.britannica.com/place/Karnal) [now in [Haryana](https://www.britannica.com/place/Haryana)], [India](https://www.britannica.com/place/India)—died February 1, 2003, in flight, over [Louisiana](https://www.britannica.com/place/Louisiana-state) and [Texas](https://www.britannica.com/place/Texas-state), U.S.) was an Indian-born American [astronaut](https://www.britannica.com/topic/astronaut) and the first woman of Indian origin to go to space. She flew two missions aboard the [space shuttle](https://www.britannica.com/technology/space-shuttle)_Columbia_: first in 1997 and in the shuttle’s final journey in 2003. She was one of seven astronauts who died when [_Columbia_ disintegrated during reentry](https://www.britannica.com/event/Columbia-disaster) into Earth’s atmosphere on February 1, 2003.

## Early life and education

Chawla studied at Tagore Baal Niketan Senior [Secondary School](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/Secondary%20School) and then completed a year of preuniversity education in 1977 at Kumari Vidyavati Anand DAV College for Women, both in Karnal. She had always been fascinated by space and flying and wanted to study aerospace engineering, so she also enrolled in a preengineering course at Dyal Singh College in Karnal for a year. Since Karnal did not have an engineering college, she moved to [Chandigarh](https://www.britannica.com/place/Chandigarh-India)to study at Punjab Engineering College. In 1982 she became the first woman to receive a degree in aeronautical engineering from the college.

Chawla moved to the [United States](https://www.britannica.com/place/United-States) in 1982 to study at the [University of Texas](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Texas) at [Arlington](https://www.britannica.com/place/Arlington-Texas) (UTA), where she received an M.S. degree in [aerospace engineering](https://www.britannica.com/technology/aerospace-engineering) in 1984. There she met Jean-Pierre Harrison, whom she married in 1983. Chawla then received a doctorate in aerospace engineering in 1988 from the [University of Colorado](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Colorado).

## Career

Chawla started working at Ames Research Center at [NASA](https://www.britannica.com/topic/NASA) in 1988. Her research focused on the [simulation](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/simulation) of air flows around aircraft in flight. In 1993 she moved to a nonprofit research organization called Overset Methods Inc. in California as vice president, working on aerodynamic optimization.

After becoming an American citizen in April 1991, Chawla applied to the NASA astronaut corps. She was selected in December 1994 and began training at the Johnson Space Center in Houston in March 1995. After a year of training, she became a crew representative for the Astronaut Office EVA/Robotics and Computer Branches, working with Robotic Situational Awareness Displays and testing software for space shuttles.

In November 1996 Chawla was selected as a mission specialist and prime robotic arm operator on mission STS-87 aboard _[Columbia](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Columbia-space-shuttle)_. STS-87 launched in November 1997, making Chawla the first woman of Indian origin to go to space. _Columbia_ made 252 orbits of Earth before returning in December 1997.

[![Image 16: The last Columbia space mission](https://cdn.britannica.com/99/85199-050-C99B45D9/David-Brown-space-shuttle-Columbia-Rick-Husband-February-1-2003.jpg?w=300)](https://cdn.britannica.com/99/85199-050-C99B45D9/David-Brown-space-shuttle-Columbia-Rick-Husband-February-1-2003.jpg)

[The last _Columbia_ space mission](https://cdn.britannica.com/99/85199-050-C99B45D9/David-Brown-space-shuttle-Columbia-Rick-Husband-February-1-2003.jpg)Crew of the 2003 _Columbia_ mission (from left): David Brown, Rick Husband, Laurel Clark, Kalpana Chawla, Michael Anderson, William McCool, and Ilan Ramon. The shuttle broke up catastrophically on February 1, 2003, killing all aboard.(more)

In July 2000 Chawla was selected for her second mission, STS-107—also aboard _[Columbia](https://www.britannica.com/event/Columbia-disaster)_—as a mission specialist. The mission was [delayed](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/delayed) several times before taking off on January 16, 2003. In space the crew conducted over 80 experiments in 16 days, working 24 hours a day in two alternating shifts. During launch, a piece of insulating foam had dislodged from a part of the shuttle and struck its left wing. This allowed gases superheated by the shuttle’s reentry into Earth’s atmosphere to enter the shuttle, and _Columbia_ disintegrated over Louisiana and Texas on February 1, 2003, killing Chawla and the rest of the crew.

## Legacy

Chawla posthumously received the Congressional Space [Medal of Honor](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Medal-of-Honor-United-States-military-decoration) in 2004 from U.S. Pres. [George W. Bush](https://www.britannica.com/biography/George-W-Bush) and the NASA Space Flight Medal and the NASA Distinguished Service Medal. The institutes she studied at honored her in many ways: UTA opened a memorial displaying one of her flight suits and photographs (all donated by her husband) in 2010, while Punjab Engineering College instituted a memorial award in her name for meritorious aerospace engineering students. The band Deep Purple wrote the song “Contact Lost” on the album _Bananas_ in honor of the _Columbia_ tragedy as Chawla had carried its albums—_Machine Head_ and _Purpendicular_—on her final mission.

NASA Opportunity for Alma Mater

At Chawla’s request, NASA started to invite two students of Tagore Baal Niketan Senior Secondary School to participate in its Summer Space Experience program from 1998 onward.

Asteroid 51826 was renamed 51826 Kalpanachawla in 2003, one of seven asteroids to be named for the crew of _Columbia_’s final mission. In 2020 the aerospace and defense company Northrop Grumman named its [International Space Station](https://www.britannica.com/topic/International-Space-Station) resupply capsule the SS _Kalpana Chawla_. Some educational institutions in India and streets in India and the United States also bear her name.

**University of Texas**, state [university](https://www.britannica.com/topic/university) system based in [Austin](https://www.britannica.com/place/Austin-Texas), [Texas](https://www.britannica.com/place/Texas-state), U.S. Branch campuses are located in [Arlington](https://www.britannica.com/place/Arlington-Texas) (founded 1895), [El Paso](https://www.britannica.com/place/El-Paso-Texas) (1913), [Edinburg](https://www.britannica.com/place/Edinburg-Texas) (Pan American branch; 1927), [Richardson](https://www.britannica.com/place/Richardson) (Dallas branch; 1961), [Odessa](https://www.britannica.com/place/Odessa-Texas) (Permian [Basin](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/Basin) branch; 1969), [San Antonio](https://www.britannica.com/place/San-Antonio-Texas) (1969), [Tyler](https://www.britannica.com/place/Tyler) (1971), and [Brownsville](https://www.britannica.com/place/Brownsville-Texas) (1973). Health science centres are located at Tyler (1947), San Antonio (1969), and [Houston](https://www.britannica.com/place/Houston) (1972); the Medical Branch at [Galveston](https://www.britannica.com/place/Galveston-Texas) (1881); the M.D. Anderson Cancer Center in Houston (1941); the Southwestern Medical Center at [Dallas](https://www.britannica.com/place/Dallas) (1943).

At Austin, the largest campus (founded 1881) in the University of Texas System, about 100 undergraduate degree programs and about 180 graduate degree programs are available in 15 schools and colleges. The [master’s degree](https://www.britannica.com/topic/master-degree) programs in theatre and architecture are especially well regarded. The university awards about 75 doctoral degrees. It also has one of the largest academic library systems in the country (eight million books). More than 85 organized research units are housed on campus, including the Center for Biological and Medical Engineering, the [Bureau](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/Bureau) of Economic Geology, the Institute for Neuroscience, and the Bureau of Business Research. Also on campus are the Texas Memorial Museum of Science and History, the Lyndon Baines Johnson Library and Museum (with the presidential papers and memorabilia of the [36th U.S. president](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Lyndon-B-Johnson)), and the Center for Studies in Texas History. Off-campus facilities include [McDonald Observatory](https://www.britannica.com/topic/McDonald-Observatory) (dedicated 1939) on Mount Locke near Fort Davis and the Marine Science Institute (1946) on the [Gulf of Mexico](https://www.britannica.com/place/Gulf-of-Mexico-Gulf-of-America) at Port Aransas. Enrollment at the Austin campus is almost 50,000, making it one of the largest university campuses in the United States; total enrollment for the system as a whole [exceeds](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/exceeds) 215,000.

Lawmakers of the republic and the state of Texas made several attempts to establish a state university, beginning in 1837. The state constitution of 1876 provided an endowment, and the state legislature in 1881 established a campus at Austin and a medical branch at Galveston. The University of Texas at Austin opened in 1883, and the Medical Branch opened at Galveston in 1891. The tower of the Main Building, a distinguishing feature of the campus, was erected in 1937. In 1966 a [student](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Charles-Whitman) atop the tower shot and killed 16 people and [wounded](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/wounded) 31 before he himself was killed by a police officer. Oil was discovered on university lands in west Texas in the early 1920s.

**Kalpana Chawla** (born March 17, 1962, [Karnal](https://www.britannica.com/place/Karnal) [now in [Haryana](https://www.britannica.com/place/Haryana)], [India](https://www.britannica.com/place/India)—died February 1, 2003, in flight, over [Louisiana](https://www.britannica.com/place/Louisiana-state) and [Texas](https://www.britannica.com/place/Texas-state), U.S.) was an Indian-born American [astronaut](https://www.britannica.com/topic/astronaut) and the first woman of Indian origin to go to space. She flew two missions aboard the [space shuttle](https://www.britannica.com/technology/space-shuttle)_Columbia_: first in 1997 and in the shuttle’s final journey in 2003. She was one of seven astronauts who died when [_Columbia_ disintegrated during reentry](https://www.britannica.com/event/Columbia-disaster) into Earth’s atmosphere on February 1, 2003.

## Early life and education

Chawla studied at Tagore Baal Niketan Senior [Secondary School](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/Secondary%20School) and then completed a year of preuniversity education in 1977 at Kumari Vidyavati Anand DAV College for Women, both in Karnal. She had always been fascinated by space and flying and wanted to study aerospace engineering, so she also enrolled in a preengineering course at Dyal Singh College in Karnal for a year. Since Karnal did not have an engineering college, she moved to [Chandigarh](https://www.britannica.com/place/Chandigarh-India)to study at Punjab Engineering College. In 1982 she became the first woman to receive a degree in aeronautical engineering from the college.

Chawla moved to the [United States](https://www.britannica.com/place/United-States) in 1982 to study at the [University of Texas](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Texas) at [Arlington](https://www.britannica.com/place/Arlington-Texas) (UTA), where she received an M.S. degree in [aerospace engineering](https://www.britannica.com/technology/aerospace-engineering) in 1984. There she met Jean-Pierre Harrison, whom she married in 1983. Chawla then received a doctorate in aerospace engineering in 1988 from the [University of Colorado](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Colorado).

## Career

Chawla started working at Ames Research Center at [NASA](https://www.britannica.com/topic/NASA) in 1988. Her research focused on the [simulation](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/simulation) of air flows around aircraft in flight. In 1993 she moved to a nonprofit research organization called Overset Methods Inc. in California as vice president, working on aerodynamic optimization.

After becoming an American citizen in April 1991, Chawla applied to the NASA astronaut corps. She was selected in December 1994 and began training at the Johnson Space Center in Houston in March 1995. After a year of training, she became a crew representative for the Astronaut Office EVA/Robotics and Computer Branches, working with Robotic Situational Awareness Displays and testing software for space shuttles.

In November 1996 Chawla was selected as a mission specialist and prime robotic arm operator on mission STS-87 aboard _[Columbia](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Columbia-space-shuttle)_. STS-87 launched in November 1997, making Chawla the first woman of Indian origin to go to space. _Columbia_ made 252 orbits of Earth before returning in December 1997.

[![Image 16: The last Columbia space mission](https://cdn.britannica.com/99/85199-050-C99B45D9/David-Brown-space-shuttle-Columbia-Rick-Husband-February-1-2003.jpg?w=300)](https://cdn.britannica.com/99/85199-050-C99B45D9/David-Brown-space-shuttle-Columbia-Rick-Husband-February-1-2003.jpg)

The shuttle broke up catastrophically on February 1, 2003, killing all aboard.(more)

In July 2000 Chawla was selected for her second mission, STS-107—also aboard _[Columbia](https://www.britannica.com/event/Columbia-disaster)_—as a mission specialist. The mission was [delayed](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/delayed) several times before taking off on January 16, 2003. In space the crew conducted over 80 experiments in 16 days, working 24 hours a day in two alternating shifts. During launch, a piece of insulating foam had dislodged from a part of the shuttle and struck its left wing. This allowed gases superheated by the shuttle’s reentry into Earth’s atmosphere to enter the shuttle, and _Columbia_ disintegrated over Louisiana and Texas on February 1, 2003, killing Chawla and the rest of the crew.

## Legacy

Chawla posthumously received the Congressional Space [Medal of Honor](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Medal-of-Honor-United-States-military-decoration) in 2004 from U.S. Pres. [George W. Bush](https://www.britannica.com/biography/George-W-Bush) and the NASA Space Flight Medal and the NASA Distinguished Service Medal. The institutes she studied at honored her in many ways: UTA opened a memorial displaying one of her flight suits and photographs (all donated by her husband) in 2010, while Punjab Engineering College instituted a memorial award in her name for meritorious aerospace engineering students. The band Deep Purple wrote the song “Contact Lost” on the album _Bananas_ in honor of the _Columbia_ tragedy as Chawla had carried its albums—_Machine Head_ and _Purpendicular_—on her final mission.

NASA Opportunity for Alma Mater

At Chawla’s request, NASA started to invite two students of Tagore Baal Niketan Senior Secondary School to participate in its Summer Space Experience program from 1998 onward.

Asteroid 51826 was renamed 51826 Kalpanachawla in 2003, one of seven asteroids to be named for the crew of _Columbia_’s final mission. In 2020 the aerospace and defense company Northrop Grumman named its [International Space Station](https://www.britannica.com/topic/International-Space-Station) resupply capsule the SS _Kalpana Chawla_. Some educational institutions in India and streets in India and the United States also bear her name.

**University of Texas**, state [university](https://www.britannica.com/topic/university) system based in [Austin](https://www.britannica.com/place/Austin-Texas), [Texas](https://www.britannica.com/place/Texas-state), U.S. Branch campuses are located in [Arlington](https://www.britannica.com/place/Arlington-Texas) (founded 1895), [El Paso](https://www.britannica.com/place/El-Paso-Texas) (1913), [Edinburg](https://www.britannica.com/place/Edinburg-Texas) (Pan American branch; 1927), [Richardson](https://www.britannica.com/place/Richardson) (Dallas branch; 1961), [Odessa](https://www.britannica.com/place/Odessa-Texas) (Permian [Basin](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/Basin) branch; 1969), [San Antonio](https://www.britannica.com/place/San-Antonio-Texas) (1969), [Tyler](https://www.britannica.com/place/Tyler) (1971), and [Brownsville](https://www.britannica.com/place/Brownsville-Texas) (1973). Health science centres are located at Tyler (1947), San Antonio (1969), and [Houston](https://www.britannica.com/place/Houston) (1972); the Medical Branch at [Galveston](https://www.britannica.com/place/Galveston-Texas) (1881); the M.D. Anderson Cancer Center in Houston (1941); the Southwestern Medical Center at [Dallas](https://www.britannica.com/place/Dallas) (1943).

At Austin, the largest campus (founded 1881) in the University of Texas System, about 100 undergraduate degree programs and about 180 graduate degree programs are available in 15 schools and colleges. The [master’s degree](https://www.britannica.com/topic/master-degree) programs in theatre and architecture are especially well regarded. The university awards about 75 doctoral degrees. It also has one of the largest academic library systems in the country (eight million books). More than 85 organized research units are housed on campus, including the Center for Biological and Medical Engineering, the [Bureau](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/Bureau) of Economic Geology, the Institute for Neuroscience, and the Bureau of Business Research. Also on campus are the Texas Memorial Museum of Science and History, the Lyndon Baines Johnson Library and Museum (with the presidential papers and memorabilia of the [36th U.S. president](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Lyndon-B-Johnson)), and the Center for Studies in Texas History. Off-campus facilities include [McDonald Observatory](https://www.britannica.com/topic/McDonald-Observatory) (dedicated 1939) on Mount Locke near Fort Davis and the Marine Science Institute (1946) on the [Gulf of Mexico](https://www.britannica.com/place/Gulf-of-Mexico-Gulf-of-America) at Port Aransas. Enrollment at the Austin campus is almost 50,000, making it one of the largest university campuses in the United States; total enrollment for the system as a whole [exceeds](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/exceeds) 215,000.

Lawmakers of the republic and the state of Texas made several attempts to establish a state university, beginning in 1837. The state constitution of 1876 provided an endowment, and the state legislature in 1881 established a campus at Austin and a medical branch at Galveston. The University of Texas at Austin opened in 1883, and the Medical Branch opened at Galveston in 1891. The tower of the Main Building, a distinguishing feature of the campus, was erected in 1937. In 1966 a [student](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Charles-Whitman) atop the tower shot and killed 16 people and [wounded](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/wounded) 31 before he himself was killed by a police officer. Oil was discovered on university lands in west Texas in the early 1920s.
